=== 0002c220 [PLATE]
Builds the draw-order list for the scrolling scene layer table: the layer slot indices sorted by ascending depth key.

Algorithm:
Fills draw_order[0 .. DAT_00069cdc-1] with the identity permutation 0,1,2,..., where DAT_00069cdc is the number of active layer slots. Then bubble-sorts that index list in place: the outer index i runs while i < DAT_00069cdc-1, the inner index j while j < DAT_00069cdc-i-1, and each step compares the depth bytes DAT_00069cfe[draw_order[j]] and DAT_00069cfe[draw_order[j+1]] as unsigned and exchanges the two entries when the first is the greater. The result is ascending by depth. The sort is a bubble sort, so slots that share a depth value keep their slot-index order. There are no callees.

Parameters:
  draw_order -- out; base of an int array with room for at least DAT_00069cdc entries, receiving the layer slot indices in draw order. No bound is checked; fdps_draw_scene_layers passes a 6-element stack array, matching the 6-slot width of the layer table.

Returns:
  Nothing. The sorted list is the caller's array.

Pool: fdps  [hard-coded game globals DAT_00069cdc and DAT_00069cfe; no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the ail set, and the only caller is game rendering code]

Rebuild note:
The sort is a hand-written bubble sort and is therefore stable: scene layer slots that share the same depth byte at DAT_00069cfe stay in slot-index order, and fdps_draw_scene_layers blits them in exactly that order, so equal-depth layers overlap in a fixed way. Rewriting this as a call to qsort (unstable) would silently reorder equal-depth layers and change what covers what.

=== 0002c327 [EOL]
Alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] (6-byte) + lea edx,[edx+0] (3-byte) filling to 16-byte boundary at 0002c330

=== 0002c330 [PLATE]
Draws one layer of the scrolling scene: fills the visible 14x9 window of 24x24 map tiles into the scene buffer, animating the tiles the layer's attribute table marks and pulsing the tiles the movement grid has marked.

Algorithm:
Copies the 14-byte blend-level ramp at 0002b280 (02 03 04 05 06 07 07 07 06 05 04 03 02 02) onto the stack, advances tile_attr past its 0x11-byte header, and steps the highlight phase counter DAT_0006015c to (DAT_0006015c + 1) % 0x38 -- once per call, so once per layer rather than once per frame. If the global tick counter DAT_00069d64 has moved more than 3 ticks past the latch DAT_00060164, flips the two-frame animation phase DAT_00060160 with XOR 1 and re-latches the tick. Builds on the stack the four-dword blend descriptor that fdps_blit_dispatch modes 9 and 0x0a read: shade-ramp table 000653f0, blend level, inverse colour cube 000643f0, and the tint colour DAT_00060154.

Reads the layer's map size out of map_layer (tile width word at +7, tile height word at +9) and splits each pixel scroll offset into a whole tile count and a 0..23 remainder, decrementing the count and adding 24 to the remainder by hand when the offset is negative so the division floors. Then walks rows 0..8 and columns 0..13. The destination row base is scene_buf + (row * 24 + 24 - scroll_y remainder) * 0x168 + 24 - scroll_x remainder, so the window is inset 24 pixels into the 360-pixel-pitch buffer and each cell is blitted 24 pixels further right. Cell coordinates are wrapped into range modulo the map width and height (a negative remainder gets the dimension added back), giving cell = y * width + x, the 16-bit tile index at map_layer + 0xb + cell * 2, and the tile's pixel stream at tileset + *(int *)(tileset + 0xf + tile * 4).

When layer_mode is 0 every tile is blitted opaque through fdps_blit_dispatch mode 0 and neither tile_attr nor move_grid is touched. Otherwise the flag byte tile_attr[tile * 4] decides the draw. Its low three bits pick the tile animation: 1 adds the phase DAT_00060160 (0 or 1) to the tile index, a two-frame animation; 2 adds ((DAT_00069d64 >> 2) & 3) * 0x60, a four-frame animation whose frames sit 0x60 tiles apart in the tileset; every other value leaves the tile index alone. Then, if bit 0x80 of the flag byte is set, the tile is drawn translucent (mode 9) at the fixed level in tile_attr[tile * 4 + 1]. If it is clear, byte 1 of the movement grid cell (move_grid + 4 + cell * 2 + 1) decides: 0xff, the value fdps_map_grid_reset writes into every cell, means the cell is unmarked and the tile is blitted opaque; any other value means the cell is marked and the tile is drawn blended at ramp[DAT_0006015c / 4] -- mode 0x0a for layer_mode 1, mode 9 for any other non-zero layer_mode -- so marked tiles pulse between blend levels 2 and 7 out of 16.

Parameters:
  scene_buf -- the 360x240 8bpp scene buffer being composited, from fdps_draw_scene_layers; every blit goes into it and nothing else is written through it.
  map_layer -- this layer's map image, DAT_00069cb0[slot]: tile width word at +7, tile height word at +9, then width * height 16-bit tile indices from +0xb.
  tileset -- this layer's tile graphic sheet, DAT_00069c20[slot]: a dword offset table at +0xf indexed by tile index, each entry the offset from the sheet base to that tile's 24x24 RLE stream.
  move_grid -- the battle map working grid DAT_00060144 (word width, word height, then width * height 2-byte cells). Only byte 1 of a cell is read, and the cell is picked with map_layer's dimensions rather than the grid's own header.
  scroll_x -- the layer's view origin in pixels along x, may be negative; the caller derives it from the layer's scroll accumulator and the global scroll factor.
  scroll_y -- the same along y.
  tile_attr -- this layer's per-tile attribute table, DAT_00069c98[slot]: 0x11 bytes of header, then 4 bytes per tile of which byte 0 is the flag byte and byte 1 the fixed blend level. Read only when layer_mode is non-zero, but advanced past the header on every call.
  layer_mode -- the layer's mode byte, DAT_00069cf8[slot]: 0 draws the layer opaque and ignores tile_attr and move_grid; 1 draws marked and translucent tiles tinted toward DAT_00060154; any other non-zero value blends them with what is already in the buffer instead.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set, unique hash in the image; its only caller and only callee are game draw code, and it owns the game's scene rendering globals]

Rebuild note:
The highlight phase counter DAT_0006015c is advanced at the top of this function, so it steps once per drawn layer, not once per frame: the pulse of the movement-range highlight runs faster on maps with more active scene layers. Writing the obvious thing -- advancing the counter once per frame beside the DAT_00060160 tile-animation phase, which really is tick-gated here -- changes the pulse rate and decouples it from the layer count.

=== 0002c694 [EOL]
Watcom 16-byte alignment padding: two 6-byte lea-form NOPs before FUN_0002c6a0.

=== 0002c6a0 [PLATE]
Draws the map cursor overlay into the scene buffer being composited: either the bare cursor tile, or the diamond-shaped footprint of an ability's area of effect centred on the cursor, whichever the cursor-mode global selects.

Algorithm:
Dispatches on the cursor mode at 00069cd0 with a chain of equality tests; every mode draws by calling fdps_blit_cursor_tile(map_x, map_y, sprite_index, dest) once per cell, at the cursor pixel position (x = 00069cd4, y = 00069ccc) displaced by whole tiles of 0x18 = 24 pixels. The call list is hand-unrolled, one call per cell, and fdps_blit_cursor_tile itself drops any cell that falls outside the visible viewport.
  mode 1 -- the cursor tile alone, sprite 0.
  mode 2 -- the cursor tile alone, sprite 1.
  mode 3 -- radius-1 diamond: sprite 0x0e on the centre, sprites 2/3/4/5 on the tiles above/left/right/below.
  mode 4 -- radius-2 diamond, all 13 tiles: sprite 1 on the centre, 2/3/4/5 on the four tips two tiles out, 6/7/8/9 on the four diagonal tiles, a/b/c/d on the four tiles one out.
  mode 5 -- radius-3 diamond: sprite 1 on the centre, 2/3/4/5 on the four tips three tiles out, 6/7/8/9 each used twice for the eight (1,2)- and (2,1)-offset tiles of that outer ring, a/b/c/d on the four tips two tiles out, and 0x0e/0x0f on the two upper diagonal tiles with 0x11/0x10 on the lower-left and lower-right ones -- that last pair emitted out of numeric order. The four tiles orthogonally adjacent to the centre get no call at all.
  mode 6 -- draws nothing. It divides both cursor coordinates by 0x18 to get a tile position, indexes the battle grid whose base pointer is DAT_00060144 (word width, word height, then width*height 2-byte cells) as base + 4 + ((y/0x18) * width + x/0x18) * 2, and clears byte 1 of that cell -- the byte fdps_map_grid_reset fills with 0xff and fdps_map_grid_collect_marked_tiles reads to decide a cell is marked. fdps_map_cursor_move_to renders a frame at every step of a cursor move while the mode is non-zero, so this marks every tile the cursor travels across.
Mode 0, and any value above 6, falls through to the epilogue having done nothing. The mode is 0 while the cursor is hidden and 1 for the plain cursor almost everywhere in the game; the ability code sets it to the ability's area-of-effect code plus 2 -- spell record byte +4 at 00013d32 and 00027db5, item record byte +0x12 at 00025461 -- and 00027356 sets 6 just before it scrolls the cursor across the map.

Parameters:
  dest -- the scrolling scene buffer being composited this frame, 0x168 bytes per row; fdps_draw_scene_layers hands over its own buffer and it is passed straight through to fdps_blit_cursor_tile.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; game globals and game state]

Rebuild note:
The six shapes are hand-unrolled call lists, not loops, and they are not the shapes a loop would produce: mode 5 skips the four tiles orthogonally adjacent to the centre, and its lower two diagonal cells take sprites 0x11 (left) and 0x10 (right) in that order, so rewriting the dispatch as a loop over a diamond, or assuming the sprite ids run in reading order, changes what appears on screen. Mode 6 is a second trap: this draw routine, called from the frame compositor, draws nothing and instead clears the marked-cell byte of the battle grid at DAT_00060144 for the tile under the cursor, so hoisting that branch out of the renderer -- or rendering a different number of frames during a cursor move -- silently changes which tiles end up marked.

=== 0002cc17 [EOL]
Watcom inter-function alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] + lea edx,[edx+0]

=== 0002cc20 [PLATE]
Draws one 24x24 sprite of the global Cusor.cel overlay sheet into the scrolling scene buffer at a map pixel position, skipping the draw entirely when that position is outside the visible viewport.

Algorithm:
Clips first and does nothing else if the clip rejects: the position must satisfy DAT_00069ce4 <= map_x < DAT_00069ce4 + 0x138 and DAT_00069ce0 <= map_y < DAT_00069ce0 + 0xc0. DAT_00069ce4 and DAT_00069ce0 are the viewport origin in map pixels, the pair fdps_battle_player_phase_loop scrolls in 0x18-pixel steps, and 0x138 x 0xc0 is the 312x192 visible window. Converts the accepted position to a scene-buffer offset as ((map_y - DAT_00069ce0) + 0x18) * 0x168 + (map_x - DAT_00069ce4) + 0x18: the scene buffer that fdps_draw_scene_layers composites is 0x168 (360) bytes per row and carries a 0x18 (24) pixel border on all four sides, so the visible window starts at pixel (24, 24). Resolves the source pixels out of the Cusor.cel image whose pointer fdps_load_global_resources leaves in DAT_000643b8, through the CEL sprite offset table of dwords at cel + 0x0f: src = cel + *(int *)(cel + sprite_index * 4 + 0xf). Passes the two pointers to fdps_blit_dispatch with width 0x18, height 0x18, pitch 0x168 and mode 0, which selects fdps_blit_rle_passthrough; transparency is structural in that kernel, an opcode that advances the destination pointer without writing, so the sheet's uncovered pixels leave whatever the map layers already put there and no colour index is treated as a key.

Cusor.cel is not a set of eighteen cursor pictures but one box-outline kit of 24x24 pieces, which is what lets the caller assemble an arbitrary tile region's outline one cell at a time: sprite 0 is a closed box and sprite 1 the same box with a gap in the middle of each side (the two cursor styles); 2, 3, 4, 5 are the box missing its bottom, right, left, top side, the caps that go on the tips of a run; 6, 7, 8, 9 are the two-sided corner pieces top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right; 0x0a, 0x0b, 0x0c, 0x0d are pairs of 3x3 corner nubs (the two top corners, the two left, the two right, the two bottom) that close the concave joints of a stepped outline; 0x0e, 0x0f, 0x10, 0x11 are those nubs singly, top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. The sheet's last two sprites, 0x12 and 0x13, are blank and unreferenced.

Parameters:
  map_x -- horizontal position in map pixels, a multiple of 24, in the same space as the viewport origin DAT_00069ce4. fdps_draw_map_cursor forms it from the cursor X global DAT_00069cd4 plus or minus multiples of 0x18.
  map_y -- vertical position in map pixels, same space and stride, from the cursor Y global DAT_00069ccc.
  sprite_index -- which piece of the kit above to draw, 0 through 0x11. Not bounds checked.
  dest -- the 360x240 scene buffer being composited, handed down from fdps_draw_scene_layers through fdps_draw_map_cursor.

Returns:
  Nothing. There is no failure path; an off-screen position is simply not drawn.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either the watcom or the ail set and the body hash is unique in the image; its only callee is fdps_blit_dispatch and its only caller is game rendering code]

Rebuild note:
The viewport test compares only the tile's top-left corner against the 312x192 window, but the blit unconditionally writes a full 24x24 block at a 360-byte pitch, so a tile accepted at the right or bottom edge writes up to 23 pixels into the scene buffer's 24-pixel border margin -- the margin is what makes that safe (max column 0x137+0x18+23 = 358 of 360, max row 0xbf+0x18+23 = 238 of 240), and it is also why cursor tiles vanish whole rather than clipping as they leave the view. Writing the obvious thing (adding extent-based partial clipping, or compositing into a tight 312x192 buffer) both changes what the player sees at the map edges and can run past the end of the destination.

=== 0002ccd0 [PLATE]
Chooses which status-effect icon to show over one battle-map unit this cycle, or reports that the unit has none.

Algorithm:
Copies the 5-byte field-offset table at 0002b28e -- 0x23, 0x22, 0x24, 0x25, 0x27, the unit record's status-effect timer bytes in icon order -- onto the stack, and forms the record pointer as [00069cd8] + unit_index * 0x50. First pass: walks the five offsets and counts how many of those record bytes are non-zero; if none are, returns -1 at once. Second pass: replaces cycle with (cycle % count) + 1, walks the same five offsets again and decrements that counter at every non-zero byte, returning the table slot whose byte drives it to zero; if the walk ends without reaching zero it returns -1. Selecting modulo the number of active effects is what makes an advancing cycle rotate through the effects a unit is carrying. The unit record's sixth status timer, +0x26, has no entry in the table and is never shown.

Parameters:
  unit_index -- index into the 0x50-byte unit record array based at 00069cd8; FUN_0002cda0 passes the unit it is drawing. Not range-checked.
  cycle -- rotation counter, reduced modulo the number of active effects to pick one of them. FUN_0002cda0 passes the global at 00060168, which it advances once every 25 unit-draw ticks. The modulo is signed, so a negative cycle yields -1 unless the remainder happens to be 0.

Returns:
  0..4 -- the slot of the effect to show, i.e. record offsets 0x23, 0x22, 0x24, 0x25 and 0x27 respectively. FUN_0002cda0 uses it directly as the frame index into the IconSts.cel sheet held at 000643d4 and blits a 0x18 x 0x0b strip 13 scanlines below the unit's cell.
  -1 -- the unit carries no active status effect, so no icon is drawn.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in any library; game global array with 0x50-byte stride]

Rebuild note:
The five status timers are visited in the order 0x23, 0x22, 0x24, 0x25, 0x27: the first two are swapped relative to the record layout, and the sixth timer at +0x26 is deliberately absent. Writing the obvious loop over offsets 0x22..0x27 swaps two icons on the map and invents a sixth frame index that IconSts.cel does not have.

=== 0002cd9e [EOL]
Alignment padding: 8b c0 (mov eax,eax), 2-byte no-op aligning next function to 0002cda0.

=== 0002cda0 [PLATE]
Draws one unit of the battle map into the scene buffer -- either its shadow or its sprite, depending on which pass fdps_draw_map_units is running -- and steps the map's shared walk-animation clock on the way past.

Algorithm:
Whenever the frame tick DAT_00069d64 differs from the value latched in DAT_00069d18, the routine latches it and steps two counters it owns outright: the walk counter DAT_00069cc8 modulo 0x10 and the icon counter DAT_00069d1c modulo 0x19, and every time the second wraps to 0 it bumps the icon cycle DAT_00060168. The latch is what keeps this to once per tick even though fdps_draw_map_units calls the routine twice for every unit on the map.

It then forms the unit record as DAT_00069cd8 + unit_index * 0x50 and reads the portrait id at +7; 0x80 marks a record with no map sprite and returns at once. Tile position comes from the bytes at +0 and +1 multiplied by 0x18, facing from +3, the sub-tile step counter from +4 and the status byte from +5, whose bit 0 is the retired flag -- a retired unit draws nothing. Facing 0/1/2/3 selects a per-step displacement of (0,+4)/(-4,0)/(0,-4)/(+4,0), multiplied by the step counter and added to the tile position, so a unit walking between tiles is drawn 4 pixels along for each of the six steps that make up a tile; y additionally takes a fixed -6, because the sprites stand taller than their 24-pixel tile.

The walk frame is DAT_00069cc8 / 4 with 3 folded back to 1, so the three sprites of a facing play 0, 1, 2, 1. A unit carrying the paralysis counter at record +0x26 is pinned to frame 0 and displaced by DAT_00069cc8 % 2 pixels in x instead, which makes it shiver in place.

Nothing is drawn unless DAT_00069ce4 - 0x18 < x < DAT_00069ce4 + 0x138, the camera's horizontal window. The destination pointer is dest_base_offset + (y - DAT_00069ce0 + 0x18) * 0x168 + (x - DAT_00069ce4 + 0x18): pitch 0x168, with a one-tile border on both axes.

With the pass byte DAT_0006014c set, fdps_draw_map_units is in its shadow pass. The vertical window is DAT_00069ce0 - 0x1a < y < DAT_00069ce0 + 0xbe, two pixels lower than the sprite pass because the shadow is laid down two scanlines below the cell (dst + 0x2d0). Portrait ids 0x8e, 0x69, 0x6a, 0x24-0x27 and 0x3c-0x3e cast no shadow and return here. The shadow sprite comes from the global Shadow.cel sheet at DAT_000643dc through the standard CEL offset table at +0x0f, indexed by the walk frame -- or fixed at sprite 1 when status bit 0x80 says the unit has already acted this turn. Either way it goes down through fdps_blit_dispatch mode 9 (translucent) with the blend descriptor { shade ramps at 0x000653f0, level 0xa, inverse colour cube at 0x000643f0 }.

With the pass byte clear it is the sprite pass, windowed at DAT_00069ce0 - 0x18 < y < DAT_00069ce0 + 0xc0. The sprite index is record[2] * 0xc + facing * 3 + frame: record +2 holds the unit's slot in the sprite cache at DAT_00060138, which fdps_cache_cel_sprite_group filled from the portrait id, twelve sprites to a slot as four facings of three frames, and the cache's own offset table starts at its base rather than at +0x0f. A unit that has already acted (status bit 0x80) is drawn at frame 1 through mode 11, alpha-blended half-way into palette colour 0 with the descriptor's level set to 8, so it reads as greyed out; portrait ids 0x69, 0x6a and 0x24-0x27 go through mode 9 at level 7, so they read as semi-transparent; everything else is an opaque mode 0 blit. Then fdps_unit_select_status_icon(unit_index, DAT_00060168) picks an ailment icon, and any answer other than -1 blits a 0x18 by 0x0b strip out of the global IconSts.cel sheet at DAT_000643d4, 13 scanlines below the top of the unit's cell.

Every sprite blit is 0x18 by 0x18 at pitch 0x168; only the status icon is smaller.

Parameters:
  unit_index -- index into the 0x50-byte unit record array based at DAT_00069cd8, 0 .. DAT_00060150 - 1. fdps_draw_map_units passes every live index in turn, once per pass; FUN_00015860 passes the single unit standing under the map cursor.
  dest_base_offset -- base address of the destination surface, pitch 0x168. fdps_draw_map_units forwards the scene buffer it was handed; FUN_00015860 passes its own 360x240 page.
  flag -- overwritten with 0 at 0002cdba before any read, so no value passed here can be observed. fdps_draw_map_units forwards its own second argument, FUN_00015860 passes 0.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either library set and a hash unique in the image; its whole state is game globals and the game's 0x50-byte unit record, and every callee is game code]

Rebuild note:
The map's walk-animation clock lives inside this per-unit draw: DAT_00069cc8, DAT_00069d1c and DAT_00060168 are stepped here and nowhere else in the program, and only when the frame tick DAT_00069d64 has moved since the previous call (the latch is DAT_00069d18). Writing the obvious thing -- stepping the counter at the top of the function without the tick latch, or hoisting the step out into the frame loop -- runs the walk cycle at twice the unit count per frame, or stops it on the frames where only FUN_00015860 draws. Separately, the two passes clip against vertical windows two pixels apart (DAT_00069ce0-0x18 .. +0xc0 for the sprite, -0x1a .. +0xbe for the shadow, which is blitted two scanlines lower); folding them into one shared test makes shadows appear and disappear a row early or late along the top and bottom edges of the view.

=== 0002d204 [EOL]
Alignment padding: two 6-byte LEA NOP forms filling to the 16-byte entry of fdps_get_unit_record.

=== 0002d210 [PLATE]

=== 0002d240 [PLATE]
Draws every unit on the map into the scene buffer, all the shadows first and then the unit sprites.

Algorithm:
Walks the unit table twice, each pass running index 0 up to the live unit count in DAT_00060150 and calling fdps_draw_map_unit(index, dest_base_offset, flag), which draws one unit out of the 0x50-byte record array based at DAT_00069cd8. Which of the two things fdps_draw_map_unit draws is selected by the pass byte DAT_0006014c, which this function is the only writer of and fdps_draw_map_unit the only reader of. The first pass sets it to 1, so fdps_draw_map_unit blits the unit's shadow from the global Shadow.cel sheet at DAT_000643dc, translucently and two scanlines below the unit's cell. The second pass clears it to 0, so fdps_draw_map_unit blits the unit's own 0x18 by 0x18 sprite from the map sprite sheet at DAT_00060138 and, above it, whatever status icon fdps_unit_select_status_icon picks. Both arguments are forwarded unchanged on every call. The pass byte is left at 0 on the way out.

Splitting the work this way is what keeps a unit drawn later in the table from casting its shadow over a unit drawn earlier: every shadow is on the surface before the first sprite goes down.

Parameters:
  dest_base_offset -- base address of the destination scene buffer, whose pitch is 0x168 bytes; forwarded to fdps_draw_map_unit, which turns it into a per-unit destination pointer. The only caller, fdps_draw_scene_layers, passes the buffer it was handed.
  flag -- forwarded as fdps_draw_map_unit's third argument; only its low byte is read. The only caller passes 0, and fdps_draw_map_unit overwrites that argument with 0 before ever reading it, so nothing passed here has any effect.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the ail set; its whole state is two game globals and its only callee is game code]

Rebuild note:
The two sweeps must stay separate sweeps. Collapsing them into one loop that draws each unit's shadow and sprite together -- the obvious simplification, since the pass byte is only read inside the callee -- lets a unit further down the table drop its translucent shadow on top of a unit already drawn, which the original never does because every shadow is blitted before the first sprite.

=== 0002d360 [PLATE]
Walks one battle-map unit one tile down the screen, playing the six-step walk animation and scrolling the view to keep up.

Algorithm:
Resolves the unit's 0x50-byte record as DAT_00069cd8 + unit_index * 0x50, then takes two pixel measurements before it starts: the map's full height, from the tile-height word at [DAT_00069cb0]+9 times 0x18, and the unit's starting pixel row, from its tile y at record+1 times 0x18. Writes 0 into the facing byte at record+3 -- the code fdps_unit_face_target uses for facing down. Then runs six passes with the walk sub-step counter at record+4 holding 1..6; six passes of 4 pixels make one 0x18-pixel tile. Each pass scrolls the view down by 4 (DAT_00069ce0) while the unit is more than 0x78 pixels below the top of the view and the view has not yet hit the bottom of the map (map height in pixels minus the 0xc0-pixel view height), advances the view pixel row DAT_00069ccc by 4, and calls fdps_render_view_frame unless the scancode latch that fdps_keyboard_scancode_ptr points at holds 2 or 3, the two keys that fast-forward movement. After the loop it draws one catch-up frame if the latch holds 2 -- but not if it holds 3, which skips drawing entirely. It then commits the move by incrementing the tile y at record+1, clears record+4, and reports the arrival tile to fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event as (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18, 0), so a scripted chapter event sitting on that tile is queued for the battle loop.

One of the four per-direction step routines fdps_animate_move_path dispatches to; the others are fdps_walk_step_up (0002d480), 0002d590 (direction 1, -x) and 0002d6a0 (direction 3, +x).

Parameters:
  unit_index -- index into the 0x50-byte unit record array based at DAT_00069cd8; fdps_animate_move_path passes its own unit_index through unchanged.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no fid candidate in either library; called only by fdps_animate_move_path]

Rebuild note:
Two places where the obvious rewrite is not what the original does. The arrival tile handed to fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event comes from the view/cursor globals (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18), not from the unit record that was just updated -- writing record[0], record[1] instead only agrees while the view is locked on the moving unit. And the post-loop catch-up frame is drawn on scancode 2 only, while the in-loop skip covers both 2 and 3; folding the tail test into the same 'if fast-forward' condition loses one rendered frame per tile step for key 2, or adds one for key 3.

=== 0002d480 [PLATE]
Walks one battle-map unit one tile up the screen, playing the six-step walk animation and scrolling the view to keep up.

Algorithm:
Resolves the unit's 0x50-byte record as DAT_00069cd8 + unit_index * 0x50, and reads the unit's starting pixel row once, before anything moves, as the tile y at record+1 times 0x18. Writes 2 into the facing byte at record+3 -- the code fdps_unit_face_target uses for facing up, and the one fdps_draw_map_unit turns into a per-step displacement of (0, -4). Then runs six passes with the walk sub-step counter at record+4 holding 1..6; six passes of 4 pixels make one 0x18-pixel tile. Each pass scrolls the view up by 4 (the scroll-y global DAT_00069ce0) while that starting row sits less than 0x30 pixels -- two tiles -- below the view's top edge and the view has not reached row 0; moves the map cursor pixel row DAT_00069ccc back by 4, which is the moving unit's own on-screen position; and calls fdps_render_view_frame unless the scancode latch that fdps_keyboard_scancode_ptr points at holds 2 or 3, the two keys that fast-forward movement. After the loop it draws one catch-up frame if the latch holds 2 -- but not if it holds 3, which skips drawing entirely. It then commits the move by decrementing the tile y at record+1, clears record+4, and reports the arrival tile to fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event as (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18, 0), so a scripted chapter event sitting on that tile is queued for the battle loop. Like the leftward step at 0002d590 and unlike the downward one at 0002d360, this direction needs no map extent to clamp against: running off the top edge is stopped by the DAT_00069ce0 >= 4 test alone.

Parameters:
  unit_index -- index into the 0x50-byte unit record array based at DAT_00069cd8; fdps_animate_move_path passes its own unit_index through unchanged.

Returns:
  Nothing; EAX is not loaded before the epilogue.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set, unique hash in the image; indexes the game's own 0x50-byte unit records and shares the map cursor and viewport globals with the rest of the map code]

Rebuild note:
The viewport-follow test compares the unit's pixel row as latched before the step (record byte +1 * 0x18, read once at 0002d49a-0002d4a8) against the live viewport origin DAT_00069ce0, not against the cursor position DAT_00069ccc that the loop is decrementing; recomputing it live each pass makes the gap shrink by 8 per pass instead of by 4, so the view scrolls through all six passes instead of stopping the moment the unit's starting tile sits 0x30 pixels below the view top. The arrival tile handed to fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event comes from the cursor globals (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18), not from the record that was just updated -- writing record[0], record[1] instead only agrees while the view is locked on the moving unit. And the two fast-forward scancodes are not interchangeable: 2 and 3 both suppress the per-pass redraw, but only 2 gets the single catch-up repaint after the loop (0002d527-0002d53d), so folding them into one test collapses the game's two movement speeds into one.

=== 0002d6a0 [PLATE]
Walks one battle-map unit one tile to the right (+x), playing its six-step walk animation and dragging the map cursor and the camera along with it.

Algorithm:
Forms the unit record as DAT_00069cd8 + unit_index * 0x50, reads the map's width in tiles from the signed word at offset 7 of the map header DAT_00069cb0 points at and scales it to pixels with the 0x18 tile size, and latches the unit's starting pixel x as record byte 0 (tile x) * 0x18. That latch is taken once, before the loop, and is not refreshed as the sub-step counter advances. Writes 3 into the facing byte at record +3, the code fdps_draw_map_unit reads as the (+4, 0) per-step displacement.
It then runs the sub-tile step counter at record +4 from 1 through 6. On each step: the camera origin DAT_00069ce4 scrolls 4 pixels right, but only while the latched pixel x sits more than 0xf0 pixels right of it and the camera has not yet reached map_pixel_width - 0x138 (0x138 is the camera's horizontal window width); the map cursor's pixel x at DAT_00069cd4 advances 4 pixels unconditionally, so the cursor keeps up with the unit; and fdps_render_view_frame draws the frame unless the keyboard latch that fdps_keyboard_scancode_ptr points at holds scancode 2 or 3, the game's two fast-forward keys.
After the sixth step one frame is still drawn when the latch holds 2, while a latch of 3 leaves the whole step undrawn. Record byte 0, the unit's tile x, is then incremented, the step counter at record +4 is cleared to 0, and fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event is called with the map cursor scaled back down to tile coordinates (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18) and trigger kind 0, so a chapter event sitting on the tile just stepped onto is queued.
This is one of the four per-direction step players fdps_animate_move_path dispatches to: fdps_animate_move_step_down handles direction code 0 (+y), fdps_animate_move_step_left code 1 (-x), fdps_walk_step_up code 2 (-y), and this one code 3 (+x) -- and, being the dispatcher's else branch, any other code as well.

Parameters:
  unit_index -- index into the array of 0x50-byte unit records based at DAT_00069cd8 of the unit taking the step. fdps_animate_move_path passes its own unit_index straight through. Not bounds checked.

Returns:
  Nothing. EAX is never loaded with a result before the epilogue.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit; drives the game's own unit array and map camera globals, and its only caller is fdps_animate_move_path]

Rebuild note:
Two places where the obvious rewrite is not what the original does. The camera-follow test compares the unit's pixel column as latched once before the loop (record byte 0 * 0x18, read at 0002d6ca-0002d6d7) against the live camera origin DAT_00069ce4; writing the natural thing -- recomputing the unit's drawn x each frame as tile_x * 0x18 + step * 4 -- makes the camera start scrolling up to one sub-step early, because the drawn position advances 4 pixels a frame while the latched value does not. And the arrival tile handed to fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event comes from the map cursor globals (DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18, DAT_00069ccc / 0x18), not from the unit record's own tile bytes the routine has just incremented; writing the obvious record[0]/record[1] instead reports a different tile whenever the cursor is not sitting on the walking unit, and silently loses the y coordinate the cursor carries.

=== 0002dc20 [PLATE]

Its guard at 0002dc8f compares the out_record pointer with 0, but out_record was already dereferenced at 0002dc34, so a null pointer would have faulted long before; the intent was plainly *out_record == 0 (no unit found). Writing that obvious C revives the scan, and callers that read the record on a -1 return -- 0001ff60 reads byte +7 of it to print a name -- would start getting a party-roster record for a character who is not on the map instead of a null pointer.

=== 0002df90 [PLATE]
Moves the battle unit-record array to a fresh, randomly displaced heap address and erases the copy left behind, so nothing outside the game can keep a fixed address on the unit records.

Algorithm:
1. Calls rand() and mallocs (rand() % 0x400) + 1 bytes as a scratch block, which it holds for the rest of the routine. The remainder is taken with a signed IDIV by 0x400 after SAR EDX,0x1f, so over the 0..0x7fff that rand() returns the scratch size is 1..0x400.
2. Reads the unit count at 0x00060150 and mallocs (count + 1) * 0x50 bytes -- one 0x50-byte unit record more than the live array. The scratch block is still held, so this allocation lands a random distance away from wherever the old one sat.
3. memmove(new_block, DAT_00069cd8, (count + 1) * 0x50): the full length of the NEW block, not the length of the source.
4. memset(DAT_00069cd8, 0, count * 0x50), wiping the old array before it goes back to the heap.
5. free(DAT_00069cd8), then free(scratch).
6. Publishes the new block in DAT_00069cd8. The count at 0x00060150 is never written, so the array does not gain an entry: this is a move, not a resize.

The two mechanisms only make sense together -- holding a randomly sized block across the allocation moves the array on every call, and zeroing the old storage destroys the stale copy that would otherwise survive in the freed block. fdps_battle_unit_turn, fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase and FUN_00012960 all call it at the top of each unit iteration and immediately re-resolve their record pointer through fdps_get_unit_record, so the array never sits at one address for long.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  Nothing. EAX still holds the new block pointer at the RET, but the address is published through DAT_00069cd8 and every call site overwrites EAX on the next instruction.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either library and the body hash is unique in the image; the whole body is bookkeeping over two FDPS globals -- the unit count at 0x00060150 and the unit array pointer at 0x00069cd8 -- with the game's hard-coded 0x50-byte record stride, consuming malloc/memmove/memset/free/rand as a stack-convention client]

Rebuild note:
The copy length and the wipe length deliberately disagree by one record, and neither may be "corrected". When FUN_000232b0 sized the old block last it is exactly count * 0x50 bytes, so the memmove reads 0x50 bytes past the end of that allocation and fills the spare tail slot with heap garbage; when this routine itself sized it, the old block is (count + 1) * 0x50 and the memset leaves its final record unzeroed. Writing memmove(new, old, count * 0x50) or memset over the whole allocation is the obvious C and is a behaviour change. Callers must also re-read every unit record pointer after this call: a pointer held across it points into freed, zeroed memory.

=== 0002e5e0 [PLATE]
Paints a solid square of one palette colour directly into the visible mode-13h VGA screen.

Algorithm:
Computes the top-left destination as 0xa0000 + y * 0x140 + x -- the VGA graphics aperture plus the 320-byte mode-13h scanline pitch -- and keeps it in a local. Then loops i from 0 while i < cell_pitch - 1, calling memset(dst, color, cell_pitch - 1) once per iteration and advancing dst by 0x140 to the next scanline. The square it paints is therefore cell_pitch-1 pixels wide and cell_pitch-1 pixels tall, one pixel short of cell_pitch in each direction. There is no clipping and no bounds check: x, y and cell_pitch are used exactly as given, so a run that passes column 319 spills into the following scanline.

Parameters:
  x -- screen pixel column of the square's left edge, 0..319 for an on-screen result; fdps_battle_map_overview passes 160 + tile_x * cell_pitch - (map_width_in_tiles * cell_pitch) / 2.
  y -- screen pixel row of the square's top edge, 0..199 for an on-screen result; fdps_battle_map_overview passes 100 + tile_y * cell_pitch - (map_height_in_tiles * cell_pitch) / 2.
  color -- VGA palette index, passed straight to memset so only the low byte matters. fdps_battle_map_overview uses a per-side base colour plus a 0..7 pulse counter for unit markers, and 0x82 plus that counter for the cursor marker.
  cell_pitch -- spacing in pixels between adjacent squares; the square drawn is cell_pitch-1 on a side. fdps_battle_map_overview passes its pixels-per-tile zoom step, 4 normally and 3 for maps taller than 0x28 tiles.

=== 0002f240 [PLATE]
Uploads a contiguous run of VGA DAC palette entries from three separate per-channel byte arrays, after waiting for vertical retrace so the change lands during blanking.

Algorithm:
Spins on inp(0x3da) -- the VGA Input Status #1 register -- until bit 3, the vertical-retrace-active flag, reads as set; the wait happens once, before any entry is written, so a call made while retrace is already active proceeds immediately. Then for i from 0 while i < count: writes i + first_index to the DAC write-index port 0x3c8 through outp, then writes red[i], green[i] and blue[i] to the DAC data port 0x3c9 in that order. The index port is rewritten for every entry instead of relying on the DAC's own auto-increment. The channel bytes are passed through unchanged: unlike fdps_set_palette_range there is no per-channel bias and no clamp to 0x3f, and the DAC simply ignores the top two bits of each byte. The loop bound is a signed JL, so a count of zero or less writes nothing and the retrace wait is the call's only effect.

Parameters:
  first_index -- DAC entry the run starts at, 0..255. fdps_cycle_scene_palette passes fixed high indices such as 0xf0 and 0xf6.
  red -- pointer to count consecutive red bytes, one per DAC entry.
  green -- pointer to count consecutive green bytes, one per DAC entry.
  blue -- pointer to count consecutive blue bytes, one per DAC entry. The caller aims all three at per-channel ramp arrays it copied onto its own stack, displaced by a rotating phase offset, which is what makes the colours cycle.
  count -- how many consecutive DAC entries to program; the caller passes 5, 9 and 15.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and a body hash unique in the image; the only caller is game code and the only callees are the shared inp/outp port primitives, and no CRT or AIL routine drives the VGA DAC]

=== 0002f390 [PLATE]
Blits a rectangular block of 8bpp pixels between two surfaces of independent pitch, skipping every source byte that is 0 so that palette index 0 reads as transparent.

Algorithm:
Copies src and dst into the stack cursors at [EBP-0x8] and [EBP-0x4], leaving the caller's pointers untouched, then runs the row counter [EBP-0x14] from 0 while it is less than height. For each row it runs the column counter [EBP-0xc] from 0 while it is less than width, loads src_cursor[x] zero-extended into the pixel local at [EBP-0x10], and stores that byte to dst_cursor[x] only when it is non-zero; a zero source byte is the transparency key and leaves the destination pixel as it was. After each row it adds src_stride to the source cursor and dst_stride to the destination cursor, which is what lets the two buffers have different pitches. Both loop tests are signed JL, so a width or height of 0 or less transfers nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check of any kind -- the callers do the clamping, as FUN_00019250 does when it refuses to call with coord above 0x7d. Calls nothing and touches no global.

This is the colour-keyed counterpart of fdps_blit_rect at 0x0002f2f0, and the two are not interchangeable in two ways: this one tests every pixel instead of running memmove over the row, and a src_stride of 0 is not a fill mode here -- it simply makes every destination row draw from the same source row.

Parameters:
  src -- pointer to the top-left pixel of the source rectangle, 8 bits per pixel, palette indices with 0 meaning transparent
  src_stride -- source pitch in bytes, added to the source cursor once per row; the full width of the source sheet, which is normally larger than width (0x75 from FUN_00017740, 0x7d from FUN_00019250)
  dst -- pointer to the top-left pixel of the destination rectangle in the surface being composed
  dst_stride -- destination pitch in bytes, added to the destination cursor once per row
  width -- pixels per row to consider, 0 or less transfers nothing
  height -- rows to consider, 0 or less transfers nothing

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; all ten references are direct calls from game code, and nothing in CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387 is a strided colour-keyed pixel copy]

Rebuild note:
The destination is read-modify-write, not overwrite: source bytes equal to 0 are skipped entirely, so the pixels underneath survive. Rewriting this row loop as the obvious memcpy/memmove per row -- which is what its sibling fdps_blit_rect at 0x0002f2f0 does, with the same six-argument signature -- would paint colour 0 over the background and erase whatever the previous blits had put there. The second trap is inherited from that sibling: fdps_blit_rect treats src_stride == 0 as a fill mode where the first argument is a fill byte rather than a pointer, and this function has no such branch, so carrying that special case over while writing the transparent version would dereference a colour value as a pointer.

=== 0002f410 [PLATE]
Plays the box screen transition between two pictures: a rectangle of the outgoing picture shrinks toward the centre, or a rectangle of the incoming picture grows out of the centre, one delayed frame at a time.

Algorithm:
Allocates two width*height scratch buffers with malloc, neither result checked, and snapshots the rectangle currently sitting on dst into the second one with fdps_blit_rect, so the outgoing picture survives the animation. Both scratch buffers are packed: every blit into or out of them passes width as the stride, whatever dst_pitch is.
style == 0, the outgoing picture closes in. cur_w/cur_h start at width/height and the centring offset at 0. While 2*step_x <= cur_w and 2*step_y <= cur_h, each pass rebuilds the frame from scratch: blit the whole of src into buffer A, blit the cur_w x cur_h rectangle of the snapshot at the current offset over it, present buffer A to dst, then delay(frame_delay). cur_w then drops by 2*step_x, cur_h by 2*step_y, and the offset advances by step_y*width + step_x, so the surviving rectangle of the outgoing picture keeps its centre as it shrinks.
style != 0, the incoming picture opens out. The frame count is min(width / (2*step_x), height / (2*step_y)), with one subtracted from either term that divides evenly, so the animation deliberately stops one step short of covering the whole rectangle. The rectangle starts at offset (steps*step_x, steps*step_y) sized (width - 2*steps*step_x) x (height - 2*steps*step_y). Each pass: memmove the snapshot over buffer A, blit the matching rectangle of src into buffer A at that position, present buffer A to dst, delay(frame_delay); the rectangle then grows by 2*step_x and 2*step_y while its origin walks back by (step_x, step_y), and the counter is decremented.
Both paths finish with one full fdps_blit_rect of src onto dst, which is what actually completes the transition, then free both scratch buffers.

Parameters:
  src -- the incoming picture, an 8bpp image of at least width x height
  src_pitch -- row stride of src in bytes
  dst -- the target surface; it carries the outgoing picture on entry, because the opening blit reads the rectangle back off it
  dst_pitch -- row stride of dst in bytes
  width -- rectangle width in pixels; also the stride of both scratch buffers and, times height, their malloc size
  height -- rectangle height in pixels
  step_x -- how far each vertical edge of the rectangle moves per frame; the rectangle's width changes by twice this. Must not be 0: style 0 would loop forever and style != 0 divides by 2*step_x
  step_y -- the same for the horizontal edges, with the same restriction
  frame_delay -- handed straight to the CRT delay() between frames
  style -- 0 shrinks the outgoing picture toward the centre; any other value grows the incoming picture out of the centre

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; calls fdps_blit_rect, a symbol only the game's own code can reference]

Rebuild note:
In the style != 0 path the frame count subtracts one whenever the extent divides evenly by twice the step, so the animation stops one step short and the trailing full blit is what finishes it. Writing the obvious steps = width / (2*step_x) adds a frame that paints the complete incoming picture plus an extra delay(), and the closing blit then repeats that same picture.

=== 0002f6c7 [EOL]

=== 0002f6d0 [PLATE]
Plays one of eight sliding screen transitions from a source image to a destination rectangle: four directions, each available either as the new image sliding in over the old picture or as the old picture sliding away to uncover the new one.

Algorithm:
Allocates two width*height scratch buffers with malloc and never checks either for NULL: a compose buffer for the frame being assembled, and a snapshot buffer that immediately receives a copy of the destination rectangle through fdps_blit_rect, i.e. the picture that was on screen when the transition started. Both are packed at pitch = width. Both are allocated and the snapshot is taken even for the four styles that never read them.
Dispatches on style; the compare is unsigned against 7, so any other value (a negative one included) skips every branch and drops straight to the final blit. Each branch runs i = step, 2*step, ... while i is below height (styles 0-3) or below width (styles 4-7), draws one frame with fdps_blit_rect, then calls delay(frame_delay). The last partial step is never drawn.
  style 0 -- rows 0..i of dst take the bottom i rows of src: the new image descends into view from the top edge while the old picture stays put underneath.
  style 1 -- the compose buffer takes the snapshot shifted up by i rows plus the bottom i rows of src left where they belong, then goes to dst whole: the old picture slides off the top edge and uncovers the new one.
  style 2 -- rows height-i..height of dst take the top i rows of src: the new image rises into view from the bottom edge.
  style 3 -- the compose buffer takes the top i rows of src in place plus the snapshot shifted down by i rows: the old picture slides off the bottom edge.
  style 4 -- columns 0..i of dst take the rightmost i columns of src: the new image slides in from the left edge.
  style 5 -- the compose buffer takes the snapshot shifted left by i columns plus the rightmost i columns of src in place: the old picture slides off the left edge.
  style 6 -- the horizontal counterpart of style 2, the new image arriving from the right edge, but the destination it anchors on is dst + (height - i) where every other horizontal branch works in columns of width. See the rebuild note.
  style 7 -- the compose buffer takes the leftmost i columns of src in place plus the snapshot shifted right by i columns: the old picture slides off the right edge.
Ends every path with one full-rectangle blit of src over dst, so the destination always holds the complete new image whatever the style was, then frees the compose and snapshot buffers.

Parameters:
  src -- the incoming 8bpp image, read with src_pitch as its row stride
  src_pitch -- byte stride of one row of src
  dst -- the destination surface, holding the outgoing picture on entry and the whole of src on return; written with dst_pitch as its row stride, and read once at the start to take the snapshot
  dst_pitch -- byte stride of one row of dst
  width -- width in bytes/pixels of the rectangle being transitioned; also the packed pitch of both scratch buffers, and the loop bound of styles 4-7
  height -- height in rows of the rectangle; the loop bound of styles 0-3
  step -- pixels or rows advanced per frame; also the position of the first frame drawn
  frame_delay -- milliseconds handed to the CRT delay() after each frame
  style -- which of the eight effects to run, 0-7; anything else does the final blit with no animation

Returns:
  nothing.

Pool: fdps  [game presentation code: draws only through fdps_blit_rect, which library objects cannot reference, and merely consumes malloc/free/delay; no Function ID hit and a unique hash in the image]

Rebuild note:
Style 6 anchors its destination at dst + (height - i) while its loop counts i up to width. Writing the obvious dst + (width - i) draws a different picture on any rectangle that is not square, and it also removes an out-of-bounds write the original has: on a 320x200 rectangle i runs past 200, so the original starts writing in front of dst. Keep height here, and do not add a bounds guard.

=== 0002fb80 [PLATE]
Mosaic screen transition: shuffles a table of every cell of a grid_cols x grid_rows phase grid and, one shuffled cell at a time, blits every block belonging to that phase from src to dst, pausing with delay() after each cell so the image appears in random patches.
Pool: fdps  [called by game code, calls fdps_blit_rect; no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ail set]
Evidence: Both callers are game-side screen code (fdps_load_game_screen, FUN_000241e0) and it calls the game's fdps_blit_rect at 0002f2f0, which library objects cannot do; malloc/free/rand/delay are its only vendor calls, the application usage pattern. full_hash a78787bdeb7cc69f is unique in the image and absent from ailv3.lib, and 689 bytes of parameterised nested loops rule out a linker or compiler product.
Name: no library symbol identified; fdps_ + snake_case describing the effect the code produces.
Boundary: 0002fb80-0002fe30, Watcom prologue at the entry and the matching epilogue RET at 0002fe30; the 15 bytes after it are LEA-form alignment padding before FUN_0002fe40.
Signature: __cdecl, eleven 32-bit stack arguments at [EBP+0x14]..[EBP+0x3c] (dst, dst_pitch, src, src_pitch, width, height, grid_cols, grid_rows, block_w, block_h, delay), returns void, bare RET so the caller cleans.
Details: allocates grid_cols*grid_rows four-byte entries (int16 col, int16 row) and fills them row-major. The shuffle is NOT Fisher-Yates: for each index i it draws two independent rand() values and swaps entry i with entry j = grid_cols*(rand()%grid_rows) + rand()%grid_cols, so an entry can be revisited and the permutation is not uniform. Per-phase block counts are blocks_x = ceil((width/block_w)/grid_cols) and blocks_y = ceil((height/block_h)/grid_rows). For shuffled cell (bx,by) it walks x = bx + i*grid_cols and pixel row y = block_h*(j*grid_cols + by), drawing only when x < width and y < height; source is src + y*src_pitch + x*block_w, destination is dst + y*dst_pitch + (dst_pitch ? x*block_w : 0), size block_w by block_h. delay() is called once per shuffled cell, after all of that cell's blocks, not per block row. The horizontal bound test compares a block-column index against the pixel width while the vertical one compares a pixel row against the pixel height, so the horizontal test is far looser; the real horizontal bound is the blocks_x loop count. The table is freed before returning.

=== 0002fe31 [EOL]
Watcom 16-byte alignment padding between fdps_transition_random_blocks and FUN_0002fe40

=== 0002fe40 [PLATE]
Draws a rectangular region from one 8bpp surface into another as a mosaic: each block_w x block_h cell of the region becomes one flat colour, taken from the source pixel at the middle of that cell.

Algorithm:
Divides the region into ceil(width/block_w) columns by ceil(height/block_h) rows of cells, each count computed as a signed divide plus one when the remainder is non-zero. Walks the cell rows outermost: for each row it forms the source sample row pointer src + sample_row*src_stride (sample_row starts at block_h/2 and grows by block_h), resets the sample column to block_w/2 and the destination x to 0, and shortens the band height to height - dest_y when a full block_h would overrun the region. Inside it walks the cell columns, shortening the run width to width - dest_x when a full block_w would overrun, then fills the cell by calling memset once per destination row: memset(band_row + dest_x, src_sample_byte, run_width), stepping band_row by dst_stride. After each cell the destination x advances by the run width and the sample column by block_w; if the sample column has reached width it is snapped back to width - width%block_w, the start of the trailing partial column, and the run width is set to that remainder. The same snap is applied to the sample row and the band height against height at the end of each cell row, while the destination band pointer advances by dst_stride*block_h. Nothing is read from the destination and nothing is written to the source, so src and dst may be the same surface only if the mosaic is not meant to feed back into itself.

Parameters:
  src -- base of the 8bpp surface sampled; the region's top-left pixel, not the surface's
  src_stride -- bytes between two source rows; 0x140 (320) from the only caller
  dst -- base of the 8bpp surface written; the region's top-left pixel. The only caller passes 0xa3b58, the VGA framebuffer at 0xa0000 plus 47*320+152
  dst_stride -- bytes between two destination rows; 0x140 (320) from the only caller
  width -- region width in pixels; 0x97 (151) from the only caller
  height -- region height in pixels; 0x95 (149) from the only caller
  block_w -- mosaic cell width in pixels, 1 or more
  block_h -- mosaic cell height in pixels, 1 or more. The only caller always passes block_w == block_h

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; its only caller is game code (fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window) and its only callee is the CRT memset, which is the normal direction]

Rebuild note:
The source sample position is a running accumulator that is snapped to width - width%block_w (the first pixel of the trailing partial cell) once it passes the region, not clamped to width-1; the same snap applies to rows against height. Writing the obvious src[min(row*block_h + block_h/2, height-1)*src_stride + min(col*block_w + block_w/2, width-1)] agrees everywhere except the trailing partial row or column, and only when the remainder is 2 or more but no larger than half the block: with the caller's height 149 and block_h 7, the original fills the last two-pixel band from source row 147 while the clamped form uses row 148. The same accumulator makes width%block_w == 0 leave a run width of 0 and a sample column of width on its final update; that value is never used only because the cell loop ends on that iteration, so a rewrite that keeps looping would read one pixel past the region.

=== 00030006 [EOL]

=== 00030010 [PLATE]
Alpha-blends a single constant palette colour over an 8bpp source rectangle, resolving each blended colour back to a palette index through an inverse-palette table.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit on either library set; hash unique in the image; called only from named game code]
Evidence: fid.watcom and fid.ail are both empty with zero candidates, and full_hash aa05da20779be6da has same_hash_in_image 1 and same_hash_in_ail_lib 0, so these bytes match nothing in CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387 or ailv3.lib. The only references are three static calls from fdps_play_vfs_animation and fdps_show_game_over - no function-pointer table slot, so no other module decides the pool. It calls nothing and touches no globals, no AIL state and no DOS state. The arithmetic is game-specific 8bpp palette compositing against the game's own weighted blend table and inverse-palette LUT, which is no C runtime service, and at 262 bytes with a full frame and two nested loops it is far larger than anything the linker or compiler emits, so not binary_artifact.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code; no vendor symbol to collide with, and the unique hash rules out a shape collision.
Boundary: 00030010-00030115, entry on the Watcom prologue 53 56 57 55 89 e5 / sub esp,0x1c whose four pushes explain the first argument sitting at [EBP+0x14], end on the RET closing the matching epilogue; the 10 bytes after it are LEA-form NOP padding aligning the next function to 00030120.
Signature: __cdecl, confirmed by the assembly - all ten arguments are read from [EBP+0x14] through [EBP+0x38], EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX are written before ever being read so nothing arrives in registers, and the plain RET leaves the caller to clean up. Returns nothing.

Algorithm:
blend_table is a [18][256] array of dwords holding each palette entry pre-scaled by a weight, with the three colour channels packed one per byte (channel n in bits 8n+4..8n+7 before the shift below). Rows 0..8 hold weights 0..8; rows 9..17 (dword offset 0x900 = 9*256) hold the complementary weights. To keep the row index inside 0..8 the function folds alpha: for alpha <= 8 the constant colour reads row alpha and the source pixels read row 9+alpha; for alpha > 8 alpha is replaced by 16-alpha, the constant colour reads row 9+alpha' and the source pixels read row alpha'. Either way the constant colour ends up weighted by the caller's alpha and the source pixel by 16-alpha.
The scaled constant colour is fetched once before the loops. For each pixel the scaled source colour is added to it, the sum is shifted right by 4 (dividing out the /16 of the weights) and masked with 0x000F0F0F, leaving 4 bits per channel at bits 0..3, 8..11 and 16..19. Those are folded into a 12-bit index by (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12), giving channel0 in bits 0..3, channel2 in bits 4..7 and channel1 in bits 8..11. That index selects a palette byte from the 4096-entry inverse-palette table rgb444_lut, which is stored to the destination.
Rows advance by src_stride and dst_stride; no clipping, no transparency test, every pixel in the rectangle is written.

Parameters:
src         - source 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
src_stride  - bytes to add to src per row
dst         - destination 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
dst_stride  - bytes to add to dst per row
width       - pixels per row
height      - number of rows
blend_table - base of the [18][256] dword weighted-colour table
rgb444_lut  - base of the 4096-entry packed-RGB to palette-index table
tint_color  - palette index of the constant colour being blended in
alpha       - blend weight of tint_color, 0..16 (0 = source only, 16 = tint only)

Returns:
Nothing.

=== 00030116 [EOL]
Alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] + lea edx,[edx+eiz*1+0], aligns next function to 0x30120.

=== 00030120 [PLATE]
Blits an 8bpp source rectangle into a destination surface with one constant palette colour blended over it, skipping every source pixel of palette index 0 so it reads as transparent; the colour-keyed counterpart of fdps_blit_tint_rect at 0x00030010.

Algorithm:
blend_table is an [18][256] array of dwords, the table fdps_build_palette_tables builds at DAT_000653f0: every palette entry pre-scaled by a weight, with the three channels held one per byte (red in bits 16-19, green in 8-11, blue in 0-3 of the packed word). Rows 0..8 carry weights 0..8 and rows 9..17 (dword offset 0x900 = 9*256) the complementary weights, so the row index is kept inside 0..8 by folding alpha: for alpha <= 8 the constant colour reads row alpha and the source pixels row 9+alpha; for alpha > 8 alpha is replaced by 16-alpha, the constant colour reads row 9+alpha' and the source pixels row alpha'. Either way tint_color ends up weighted by alpha and the source pixel by 16-alpha. The row base is blend_table + alpha*0x100 dwords (SHL 0xa, 0x400 bytes per row) and is computed once, after the fold.
The scaled constant colour blend_table[alpha][tint_color] is fetched once before the loops. Then height rows of width pixels each: a source byte of 0 is skipped and the destination pixel keeps what it had; any other byte has its own scaled colour added to the constant, the sum shifted right by 4 to divide out the weights, masked with 0x000F0F0F and folded into a 12-bit value by (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12), which lands green in bits 8-11, red in bits 4-7 and blue in bits 0-3 -- the order fdps_build_palette_tables fills the 4096-entry cube at DAT_000643f0 in. That value indexes rgb444_lut and the palette byte it holds is stored to the destination.
At the end of each row src_stride is added to src and dst_stride to dst, both in the caller's own argument slots. Both loop tests are signed, so a width or height of 0 or less draws nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check; the function calls nothing and touches no global.

Parameters:
  src -- top-left pixel of the source rectangle, 8bpp palette indices with 0 meaning transparent. FUN_0001cb00 passes a record of the 0x2b-by-6 gauge-bar table at DAT_000643b4.
  src_stride -- bytes added to src once per row; 0x2b from FUN_0001cb00, the full width of one gauge-bar record.
  dst -- top-left pixel of the destination rectangle in the surface being composed.
  dst_stride -- bytes added to dst once per row, the destination pitch, independent of src_stride.
  width -- pixels per row to draw; 0 or less draws nothing.
  height -- rows to draw; 0 or less draws nothing.
  blend_table -- base of the [18][256] dword weighted-colour table; DAT_000653f0 from FUN_0001cb00.
  rgb444_lut -- base of the 4096-entry inverse-palette cube indexed green:red:blue, 4 bits per channel; DAT_000643f0 from FUN_0001cb00.
  tint_color -- palette index of the constant colour blended in, 0..255. FUN_0001cb00 forwards its own blit_mode argument, which reaches here only when it is 2 or more.
  alpha -- weight of tint_color, 0..16 (0 = source only, 16 = tint only); values above 8 are mirrored onto the low half of the table.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; no CRT, AIL or DOS idiom, no callees, and the arithmetic is game-specific 8bpp palette compositing over the game's own blend table and inverse-palette cube]

Rebuild note:
The 12-bit index into the inverse-palette cube is green:red:blue, not red:green:blue: the fold (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12) at 000301ee-000301ff puts green in bits 8-11, red in 4-7 and blue in 0-3, which is the order fdps_build_palette_tables fills DAT_000643f0 in (its outer 0..15 loop is the green argument of fdps_palette_find_nearest_color, the middle loop the red one). Writing the obvious (r << 8) | (g << 4) | b here while leaving the table builder faithful swaps red and green in every blended pixel.

=== 0003022c [EOL]
4-byte alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0x0] (8d 44 20 00)

=== 00030230 [PLATE]
Alpha-blends two 8bpp source rectangles into a destination rectangle, resolving every blended colour back to a palette index through the game's inverse-palette cube. The untransparent twin of fdps_blit_blend_transparent_rect at 0x00030360, which is this same algorithm plus an index-0 mask test.

Algorithm:
When alpha is greater than 8 the two source pointers and their strides are swapped and alpha becomes 0x10 - alpha. That yields the same blend and keeps the table row index inside 0..8, which is what the two lookups below require.
blend_table is the [18][256] dword array that fdps_build_palette_tables fills at DAT_000653f0. Each entry holds one palette colour with its three 4-bit channels packed as red at bits 16-19, green at bits 8-11 and blue at bits 0-3, pre-multiplied by that row's weight; the coefficients at DAT_0002ae40 are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,16,15,14,13,12,11,10,9,8, so row alpha and row alpha+9 always sum to a weight of 16. The row base is computed once as blend_table + (alpha << 10) and the second lookup adds 0x2400, the byte offset of nine further rows.
For each of height rows and width columns it reads one byte from each source span, looks the fg byte up in row alpha and the bg byte up in row alpha+9, adds the two packed values, arithmetic-shifts the sum right by 4 to divide by the weight total and masks it with 0x0f0f0f to drop the bits that bled between channels. It then folds the three surviving nibbles into a 12-bit key as green<<8 | red<<4 | blue -- green major, which is the order fdps_build_palette_tables walks when it fills the cube -- and stores rgb444_lut[key] into the destination span. After each row fg, bg and dst each advance by their own stride.
Both loop tests are signed, so a width or height of 0 or less draws nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check; the function calls nothing and touches no global.

Parameters:
  fg -- pointer to the top-left byte of the foreground rectangle, the source whose weight is alpha; 8bpp palette indices. Callers pass a rendered CEL panel or window image.
  fg_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of fg; 0x97 or 0x12e in the callers, i.e. the panel's own packed pitch.
  bg -- pointer to the top-left byte of the background rectangle, the source whose weight is 16 - alpha. fdps_message_window_open and fdps_message_window_close pass the same address they pass as dst, blending in place.
  bg_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of bg; 0x140 (320) in all three callers.
  dst -- pointer to the top-left byte of the destination rectangle; either VGA memory (0xa3b58 from fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window) or an offscreen 320-wide page.
  dst_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of dst; 0x140 (320) in all three callers.
  width -- pixels blended per row; 0 or less blends nothing.
  height -- rows blended; 0 or less blends nothing. fdps_message_window_open clamps it to 0x49 so the sliding panel never runs off the bottom of the screen.
  blend_table -- base of the 18 x 256 dword weighted-palette table; always DAT_000653f0.
  rgb444_lut -- base of the 16x16x16 inverse-palette cube indexed green<<8 | red<<4 | blue; always DAT_000643f0.
  alpha -- weight of fg out of 16, 0..16. 0 copies bg, 16 copies fg. The callers ramp it (1,3,..,15 and 5,7,..,15) to fade a panel in or out.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; hash unique in the image, and all three callers are game code, one of them fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window]

Rebuild note:
The 12-bit key this routine builds is green-major -- green<<8 | red<<4 | blue -- not the r<<8|g<<4|b an RGB444 lookup is usually written as. It is not a bug: fdps_build_palette_tables fills DAT_000643f0 with green as the outer loop, so the cube and the key agree. Writing the obvious RGB ordering in either place alone swaps red and green in every blended pixel.

=== 00030353 [EOL]
Alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] / lea edx,[edx+0] / nop, 13 bytes to 16-byte boundary.

=== 00030360 [PLATE]
Blends one 8bpp source rectangle over a background rectangle with index-0 transparency and writes the resulting palette indices into a destination rectangle.

Algorithm:
1. Saves src and src_pitch in locals; that saved pointer is the transparency mask for the whole run and is never swapped.
2. When alpha > 8, swaps (src, src_pitch) with (back, back_pitch) and replaces alpha with 16 - alpha, so the weight taken from the first table row is always 0..8.
3. Selects the two blend rows out of blend_tables (DAT_000653f0 at both call sites): row alpha at blend_tables + alpha*0x400, and row alpha+9 at a further +0x2400. fdps_build_palette_tables fills those rows: row L holds, for each of the 256 palette indices, the entry's colour packed as red nibble in bits 16-19, green in bits 8-11, blue in bits 0-3, multiplied by the coefficient table at 0002ae40 whose 18 entries are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,16,15,14,13,12,11,10,9,8. Pairing row alpha with row alpha+9 therefore gives weights alpha and 16-alpha, which sum to 16.
4. For each row y < height, for each column x < width: leaves dst[x] untouched when the mask byte at that column is 0; otherwise adds the row-alpha entry for src[x] to the row-alpha+9 entry for back[x], shifts the sum right by 4 and masks 0x0f0f0f, which leaves the three blended 4-bit channels one per byte with no carry between them, folds them into the 12-bit key green<<8 | red<<4 | blue, and stores inverse_palette[key] into dst[x].
5. At the end of each row advances src, back and dst by their own pitches, and the mask pointer by the original src pitch.

This is the index-0-transparent member of the blend pair; fdps_blit_blend_rects at 00030230 is the same blend with no mask test.

Both callers, fdps_draw_unit_gauge and fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up, pass the same pointer for back and for dst, so the visible effect is a translucent sprite drawn onto the surface it reads through.

Parameters:
  src -- top 8bpp span, the sprite or foreground; also the transparency mask, whose zero bytes suppress the write. fdps_draw_unit_gauge passes a gauge-bar graphic of stride 0x2b, fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up a 0x28-wide sprite.
  src_pitch -- byte stride between rows of src.
  back -- 8bpp span blended underneath src; both callers pass the destination itself.
  back_pitch -- byte stride between rows of back.
  dst -- 8bpp destination span receiving the blended indices.
  dst_pitch -- byte stride between rows of dst.
  width -- columns per row.
  height -- rows.
  blend_tables -- base of the 18 x 256 dword weighted packed-colour table built by fdps_build_palette_tables; DAT_000653f0 at both call sites.
  inverse_palette -- the 16x16x16 nearest-palette-index cube built by fdps_build_palette_tables, indexed green<<8 | red<<4 | blue; DAT_000643f0 at both call sites.
  alpha -- weight of src out of 16, 0..16. 0 leaves back showing, 16 leaves src showing. Values above 8 are handled by the swap in step 2, so both halves of the range are served by table rows 0..8.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either library set and the hash is unique in the image; both callers are game bodies and nothing in the Watcom CRT or Miles AIL does paletted blending]

Rebuild note:
The index-0 transparency test reads the ORIGINAL first source, saved to [EBP-0x4] and [EBP-0x10] at 00030372 and 0003036c before the alpha > 8 swap, not the post-swap src. Writing the obvious C -- swap the two operands, then test src[x] != 0 -- masks against the background instead of the sprite for every alpha above 8, and the sprite's transparent pixels come out painted. That path is live: fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up feeds alpha = (n / 3) + 8, which crosses 8 as the floating experience number ramps up.

Stops the sound playing on one of the game's eight digital sample voices, or on all of them.

=== 00030630 [PLATE]
Starts one raw PCM block playing on the first of the game's eight AIL sample voices that is not busy, and hands the caller back the voice it used.

Algorithm:
Returns -1 at once unless both audio gates are open: the digital-driver-present flag at 0x00069d71, which fdps_audio_init sets only when AIL_install_DIG_INI succeeded, and the sound-effects-enabled flag at 0x00069d70, which fdps_audio_init sets to 1 and fdps_options_menu toggles. It then scans slots 0..7 of the sample-handle table at 0x00069d30 -- the eight handles fdps_audio_init allocated with AIL_allocate_sample_handle -- calling AIL_sample_status on each and stopping at the first whose status is not 4 (AIL's SMP_PLAYING); when all eight are still playing it returns -1. On the handle it claimed it calls AIL_init_sample, then AIL_set_sample_address(pcm_data, pcm_len), AIL_set_sample_loop_count(loop_count), AIL_set_sample_playback_rate with the global rate at 0x00069d5c that fdps_audio_set_sample_playback_rate stores, and AIL_start_sample. It returns the slot index.

This is the barest of the game's three sample-starting routines. The other two, fdps_sfx_play@000142d0 and fdps_audio_start_wav@00030a00, claim a voice by the identical eight-slot scan and then call both AIL_set_sample_type and AIL_set_sample_volume; this one calls neither, so the block plays in whatever format and at whatever volume AIL_init_sample leaves behind. It also parses no WAV header, so the caller must hand it the PCM data itself.

Parameters:
  pcm_data -- pointer to the raw PCM block to play; read from [EBP+0x14] and passed unchanged to AIL_set_sample_address as its start argument.
  pcm_len -- length of that block in bytes; read from [EBP+0x18] and passed unchanged as AIL_set_sample_address's len argument.

=== 00030829 [EOL]
