The Win%02d.dat scene scripts are numbered by the 0-based chapter index, so chapter 15's is Win14.dat. (Ghidra's label for the string starts two bytes early, over stray "EL" bytes in the inter-string padding, which is why the decompiler renders the argument as s_Win14.dat_00062156 + 2; the characters the callee sees are "Win14.dat".) The uint it returns is discarded.
  5. FUN_00039e70 revives every party unit left at 0 HP, restoring it from its maximum and charging the per-class revive cost, and finally 0xf is stored into the chapter index at DAT_00069cf4 -- chapter index 15, i.e. the player's chapter 16 -- so the village phase main runs next, and the chapter loaded after it, are chapter 16's.

Unlike most of the family it does not call fdps_battle_destroy_remaining_enemies first: chapter 15 reaches victory through 0x00037b70, which already clears the map before the duel can start.

Parameters:
  none -- main dispatches through the chapter-end handler table with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup.

Returns:
  nothing; the effects are the un-retired party, the roster writeback, the victory scene it played, the revived party and the advanced chapter index in DAT_00069cf4.

Pool: fdps  [calls only game code; its one data operand is the game resource name "Win14.dat"; it is reached from main through the game's own chapter-end handler table, and matches no Watcom or AIL library symbol]

Rebuild note:
Chapter 15's duel event (0x00037b70) retires unit records 0..8 (skipping 4) and unit record 0x34 by writing 1 into byte +5, but this end handler only un-retires records 0..8: for record 0x34 it clears byte +0x34, the behaviour-mode byte, not byte +5. Writing the obvious mirror image of the duel event -- clearing byte +5 for record 0x34 as well -- leaves unit 52 un-retired and its behaviour byte untouched, the reverse of what the original leaves behind, and changes which records FUN_00023980 treats as active in the roster writeback that runs immediately afterwards.

Rebuild note:
Two things here have to be written literally. While DAT_000640e9 is set this handler must not fall back on fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions: the accept branch retires unit 0, 蘭迪斯, along with everyone else but unit 4, so the shared check would force the defeat code 1 into DAT_00069da0 the moment the duel starts -- writing the obvious "run the default check first, then add the chapter's extra" turns chapter 19's duel into an instant Game Over. And 0x4d is a hard-coded unit index, not a handle on the unit fdps_deploy_wave has just appended: it names the challenger only while the array already holds exactly 0x4d units, that is after both the turn-6 wave-1 arrival (fdps_chapter_19_event_lancelot_joins) and the tile-triggered wave 6 have deployed. Finish the chapter before turn 6 and the challenger is appended at 0x4c instead, where the retire sweep kills him off, and the settle test on 0x4d never fires -- the chapter can no longer be ended. That is shipped behaviour and the strategy guide records it; resolving the challenger from the deployment instead would quietly fix a bug the original has.

Watcom alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] (6-byte nop) + lea edx,[edx+0] (3-byte nop), aligning FUN_0003b0b0 to 16 bytes.

=== 0003b0b0 [PLATE]
Chapter 19's chapter-end handler: closes the chapter out by undoing the duel staging with a free full recovery for the roster whenever the chapter's duel flag is up, banking the party back into the roster, playing chapter 19's victory scene and handing the game on to chapter 20. Reached through slot 18 of the chapter-end handler table based at 0x00060304, which main indexes with the chapter index in DAT_00069cf4.

Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with 8 bytes of locals.
The first step is conditional on DAT_000640e9, chapter 19's duel flag -- byte 0x11 of the 0x20-byte per-chapter event flag block at 0x000640d8 that fdps_chapter_state_reset memsets to 0 on chapter entry and that fdps_load_savegame restores from the save file. fdps_chapter_19_init calls that reset, and inside chapter 19 the only writer of the byte is fdps_chapter_19_post_action, which raises it to 1 once it has put 裘娜's duel to the player -- on both answers, accepted and declined. On accept the same post-action stages the duel by writing 1 into the status byte at +0x05 of every unit record from 0 to 0x4c except index 4, 裘娜's slot, leaving the whole party (and every enemy) marked retired while she fights the challenger alone.
When the flag is zero this routine jumps straight past the sweep. When it is non-zero it walks battle unit indices 0 .. DAT_00060150-1 (the live battle unit count), resolves each record with fdps_get_unit_record, and for every unit whose character id byte at +0x08 is 0x0b or lower -- read as an unsigned byte; ids 0x00-0x0b are the permanent roster characters, the only ids fdps_roster_add_character is ever passed, of which chapter 19 has eleven on the roster once its own init adds id 0x0b -- writes 0 over the whole status byte at +0x05, then copies max HP at +0x42 into current HP at +0x40 and max MP at +0x46 into current MP at +0x44. Bit 0 of that status byte is the retired/dead flag fdps_unit_is_retired reads, so clearing the byte undoes the staging and revives anyone who genuinely fell during the chapter; since the flag does not record which answer the player gave, declining the duel buys the party the same free revival. The HP and MP stores are belt and braces: once the status byte is clear, fdps_roster_write_back_battle_units restores both by itself. Chapter 15, which runs the same duel one chapter earlier, undoes its own staging the same way but only clears the status byte and restores nothing.
Four steps then run unconditionally. fdps_roster_write_back_battle_units copies every battle unit record over the roster record carrying the same character id, resetting the per-battle fields as it goes. fdps_icon_script_run, the IconAni.vfs event-script interpreter, is handed the ASCIIZ resource name "Win18.dat" at 0x00062194 and plays chapter 19's victory scene -- the same 0-based 18 that fdps_chapter_19_init passes as "Icon18.dat". fdps_roster_revive_fallen_members then runs the revive screen over every roster member still at 0 HP, restoring it from its maximum and charging the party gold. Last, the chapter index global DAT_00069cf4 is set to 0x13; that global is 0-based, so 0x13 selects the player's chapter 20, and it is the index every per-chapter handler table -- chapter init, post-action, chapter end -- is dispatched through afterwards.
Unlike most of the family this handler never calls fdps_battle_destroy_remaining_enemies, so the map is not swept of enemies before the scene plays; chapters 1, 2 and 15 are the only others that skip it.

Parameters:
  none -- the chapter-end handler table is dispatched through with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup.

Returns:
  nothing; the effects are the conditional free full recovery of the roster, the roster writeback, the victory scene, the paid revive screen and the advanced chapter index in DAT_00069cf4.

Pool: fdps  [reached only through the game's own chapter-end handler table; every callee is game code and the one data operand is the game resource name "Win18.dat"; Function ID matches no Watcom 10.0x or AIL library symbol and the body hash is unique in the image]

Rebuild note:
Three things about the conditional sweep. (1) It must run before fdps_roster_write_back_battle_units: that routine masks the unit status byte at +0x05 down to bit 0 and skips restoring current HP from max whenever the bit survives, so the natural "bank the party, then heal it" ordering carries the party into chapter 20 recorded as dead -- and after an accepted duel, which stamps that bit on every unit but index 4, fdps_roster_revive_fallen_members then bills the player gold to revive the entire party. (2) The character id at +0x08 is compared as an unsigned byte (MOV AL / AND EAX,0xff before CMP EAX,0xb); Watcom's plain char is signed, so declaring that field char in C would let ids 0x80 and up pass the <= 0x0b test and be healed as well. (3) The gate is "the duel offer was made", not "the duel was fought": fdps_chapter_19_post_action raises DAT_000640e9 on its decline branch too, so a player who refuses 裘娜's duel still gets the free full recovery. Rewriting the condition as "if the duel happened" -- the obvious reading of a step whose job is to undo duel staging -- silently takes that free revival away.

=== 0003b150 [PLATE]
Chapter 20's post-action handler: releases three of the tunnel map's held enemies every turn and then applies the standard win/lose test. Reached through slot 19 of the per-chapter handler table based at 0x0006028c.

Algorithm:
Reads the battle turn counter DAT_00069ce8 (fdps_chapter_state_reset sets it to 1, fdps_battle_advance_turn raises it once per turn cycle). While it is 0x11 (17) or less it calls fdps_object_set_field34_low_nibble_range three times, each time with first_index == last_index so exactly one unit is touched, and with value 0, at unit indices turn+0xc, turn+0x1d and turn+0x2e. Value 0 in the low nibble of unit record byte 0x34 is the behavior mode fdps_map_actor_behavior_step dispatches on whose handler chain ends in a step toward the nearest opposing unit; map19.dat deploys almost every unit of this map in mode 2, which fights whatever comes within reach but never advances. So over turns 1 through 17 the three runs take unit indices 13..29, 30..46 and 47..63 out of hold and send them at the party -- three per turn, 51 in all, which is the batch-by-batch enemy advance the strategy guide describes for this map. From turn 18 on the whole block has been released and the three calls are skipped.
It then falls through, on every turn, to fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions: while the battle-end code DAT_00069da0 is still 0 that routine writes 2 (chapter cleared), puts it back to 0 if any unit whose side byte +6 is 0 is not yet retired, and -- chapter 20's 0-based index 0x13 being neither 0x10 nor 0x15 -- overwrites it with 1 (game over) when unit index 0, Randis, is retired. This handler adds no condition of its own.

Unit indices:
The three constants line up with the shipped map data. map19.dat's header gives 11 player slots (byte +1) and 55 deployment records (byte +2, 0x1a bytes each from +0x83); fdps_build_map_unit_array lays the party at indices 0..10, and fdps_deploy_wave(map, 0, 1) then appends, in record order, the 54 records tagged wave 0 at indices 11..64. Those 54 are exactly the enemy roster the strategy guide lists for this chapter -- 8 level-28 units of character id 101, 13 level-18 of id 80, 10 level-17 of id 83 and 23 level-17 of id 75 -- so the live unit count DAT_00060150 is 65 when the battle opens, and 63, the highest index this handler ever writes (turn 17 through the turn+0x2e run), is inside the array. Neither this function nor fdps_object_set_field34_low_nibble_range bounds the index against DAT_00060150, and neither has to.
Three of the 54 are never released. Index 11 is deployment record 0, the map's only unit deployed in behavior mode 5 -- the scripted event walker -- standing on the bottom-left chest at tile (4,22); it is the unit the guide warns leaves that chest to go and take the treasure at (21,2), and writing mode 0 over it would cancel that script, so the schedule starts one index above it. Index 12 (record 1, tile (22,3)) and index 64 (record 54, tile (20,12)) are ordinary mode-2 units the arithmetic simply does not reach. The 55th record, 40, is tagged wave 1: map19.dat schedules no turn event at all and its one tile trigger is chapter 20's sword upgrade, fdps_chapter_20_event_upgrade_randis_sword, so that unit arrives only if the opening IconAni script Icon19.dat deploys the wave, and it would take index 65, past everything this handler writes.

Parameters:
  none -- every dispatch site (fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase at 00012a48 and 00012aff, fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase at 00012beb, fdps_battle_unit_turn at 0001584e, fdps_battle_tick_status_effects at 0001fb50) loads the chapter index DAT_00069cf4, scales it by 4 and calls through the table with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup afterwards.

Returns:
  nothing; the outcome is left in DAT_00069da0, which each caller compares against 0 immediately after the call to decide whether to break out of the phase loop.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ailv3 set; both callees drive the unit record array through fdps_get_unit_record and the game's own chapter/battle-state globals, symbols no separately compiled vendor object could reference]

=== 0003b270 [PLATE]
Chapter 22's post-action handler: the defeat test the battle loop runs after a unit has acted, reached through slot 21 (chapter index 0x15) of the per-chapter handler table based at 0006028c.

Algorithm:

Algorithm:

The second test sits in the else arm, not beside the first: when unit 3 is already retired the handler declares defeat without ever drawing message 0x14, even if unit 0x1f is gone too. Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with an 8-byte local area, then runs five steps in order.

It keeps only bit 0 of the roster copy's flag byte at +0x05 and refuses to restore HP from the maximum at +0x42 when that bit is set, so the NPC units step 2 just retired are banked as out of play rather than as live members.

Pool: fdps  [calls only game code; its one data operand is the game resource name "Win22.dat"; it is reached from main through the game's own chapter-end handler table, and the ordinary Watcom C frame rules out binary_artifact]

Rebuild note:
The NPC sweep assigns the whole flag byte -- record[0x05] = 1 -- it does not OR bit 0 in. Writing the natural record->flags |= UNIT_RETIRED leaves the 0x80 already-acted bit and any other flag bits standing on those records while FUN_00021650 runs Win22.dat against them, and the script interpreter edits unit records. The sweep must also stay where it is, before FUN_00023980: run it afterwards and the NPC units are banked into the roster as live members with their HP restored from maximum, because the roster writeback reads that same flag bit to decide.

=== 0003b3d0 [PLATE]
Chapter 24's post-action handler: the win/lose test the battle loop runs after a unit has acted, which on the way out of the chapter offers 裘娜 the wandering swordsman's duel and, when she wins it, trades her 妖刀村正 (item 0xa6) for the 妖刀正宗 (item 0xa7). Reached through slot 23 of the per-chapter handler table based at 0x0006028c.

Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with a 0xc-byte local area, then branches on DAT_000640e9, chapter 24's duel flag -- one byte of the 0x20-byte per-chapter event flag block at 0x000640d8 that fdps_chapter_state_reset clears when a chapter starts.

Flag clear, the ordinary case: it calls fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions and adds no condition of its own. That check leaves 2 (chapter cleared) in the battle-end code DAT_00069da0 once every enemy-side unit is retired, and forces 1 (game over) when unit 0, 蘭迪斯, is retired.

Flag set, the duel is running: fdps_unit_is_retired(4) -- 裘娜's battle-map slot -- and fdps_unit_is_retired(0x52), the challenger the accept branch deployed as map 23's wave 7. While both are still standing it writes nothing at all, so the battle loop keeps running the duel. Once one of them is down it calls fdps_unit_is_retired(0x52) a second time to see which:
  - challenger gone: message 0x19 through FUN_0001ff60(DAT_00060124, 0x19, 0xa0000, 0x140, 0xd0, 0, 0x6d); then fdps_unit_find_item_slot(4, 0xa6), and when 裘娜 is still carrying the 妖刀村正 fdps_unit_remove_item takes it off her, before fdps_unit_add_item(4, 0xa7) hands her the 妖刀正宗 either way.
  - 裘娜 gone: message 0x1a, the line for the duel lost, and no item changes hands.
Both outcomes set DAT_00069da0 to 2, so the chapter ends whichever way the duel went.

Then, on every entry, the offer test -- all five of: the battle turn counter DAT_00069ce8 is 0x19 (25) or less, DAT_00069da0 is 2 (the chapter has just been cleared), DAT_000640e9 is still clear, unit 4 is not retired, and fdps_unit_find_item_slot(4, 0xa6) finds the 妖刀村正 in her bag. When they all hold:
  1. fdps_deploy_wave(DAT_00069cf4, 7, 0) appends the challenger to the unit array as the current map's wave-7 record. Wave 7 is the one wave of map 23 that fdps_chapter_24_event_deploy_wave_for_turn never brings on; the waves it schedules are 2, 6, 4, 3 and 5, on turns 5, 7, 10, 13 and 15.
  2. message 0x15, then fdps_message_window_open(0x23) slides the message panel up carrying portrait 0x23, then message 0x16 drawn at 0xaa44a -- the frame buffer plus (138, 131), inside the open panel.
  3. fdps_prompt_two_choice() takes the answer; fdps_message_window_close() retracts the panel.
  4. Answer 0, accepted: message 0x17, then a sweep of unit indices 0 through DAT_00060150 - 2 that writes 1 into byte +5, the retired flag, of every record except index 4 -- fdps_get_unit_record is called for index 4 as well, its result simply discarded. The bound stops one short of the end of the array, which is where fdps_deploy_wave has just put the challenger, so 裘娜 and the challenger are the only two left standing. DAT_00069da0 then goes back to 0 and the phase loop resumes.
  5. Answer non-zero, declined: message 0x18 and nothing else; DAT_00069da0 stays 2 and the chapter ends.
  6. Either answer sets DAT_000640e9 to 1.

The retire sweep stores 1 into byte +5 rather than ORing into it, the way fdps_battle_mark_unit_done does: one store raises the retired bit 0x01 and clears the acted-this-turn bit 0x80.

DAT_00060124 is the chapter's FDETXT dialogue resource, fdetxt24.txt; DAT_00069cf4 is the map the chapter is playing, map 23, and is also the index the handler table is walked with; DAT_00060150 is the live unit count; 0xa0000 is the mode-13h frame buffer FUN_0001ff60 draws into, 0x140 its pitch, and 0xd0, 0 and 0x6d the three colour arguments it forwards to fdps_draw_glyph.

Parameters:
  none -- every dispatch site loads DAT_00069cf4, scales it by 4 and calls through the table at 0x0006028c with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup afterwards.

Returns:
  nothing; the outcome is left in DAT_00069da0, which the callers compare against 0 to decide whether to break out of the phase loop.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ail set; reached only through the game's own per-chapter handler table at 0x0006028c, and every callee is proven game code]

Rebuild note:
0x52 is a hard-coded unit index for the challenger fdps_deploy_wave has just appended, while the retire sweep that stages the duel is bounded by the live unit count DAT_00060150 - 1. The two name the same unit only while the array holds exactly 0x52 units at the moment the offer is accepted, that is after all five of map 23's turn waves have deployed (turns 5, 7, 10, 13 and 15). Clear the chapter earlier and the settle test reads a slot the challenger never occupied: the strategy guide records the shipped result, that finishing before turn 7 makes the swordsman forfeit at the end of the first turn of the duel and hand 裘娜 the 妖刀正宗 for nothing. Resolving the challenger from what the deployment actually appended would quietly fix that. Second, while DAT_000640e9 is set this handler must not fall back on fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions first: the accept branch retires unit 0, 蘭迪斯, along with everyone else but unit 4, so the shared check would force the defeat code 1 into DAT_00069da0 the moment the duel starts.

4-byte Watcom alignment padding (lea eax,[eax+eiz*1+0x0]) aligning FUN_0003b600 to 16 bytes

=== 0003b600 [PLATE]
Chapter 24's chapter-end handler: closes the chapter out by giving the twelve roster characters a free full recovery when the shared branch flag is set, clearing the battle map, banking the party back into the roster, playing chapter 24's victory scene and handing the game on to chapter 25. Reached through slot 23 of the chapter-end handler table based at 0x00060304, which main indexes with the chapter index in DAT_00069cf4.

Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with 8 bytes of locals.
The first step is conditional on the shared one-shot byte flag at DAT_000640e9; when it is zero the routine jumps straight past it. In chapter 24 that flag is raised by FUN_0003b3d0, the chapter's post-action handler, which stages the chapter's optional one-on-one duel by writing 1 into the unit status byte at +0x05 of every battle unit except index 4 -- so if the duel was fought, the whole party bar that one unit reaches the end of the chapter marked down. When the flag is non-zero this routine undoes that. It walks battle unit indices 0 .. DAT_00060150-1 (the live battle unit count), resolves each record with fdps_get_unit_record, and for every unit whose character id byte at +0x08 is 0x0b or lower -- read as an unsigned byte; indices 0x00-0x0b of FRIAPRDA.DAT, the twelve permanent roster characters -- writes 0 over the whole status byte at +0x05, then copies max HP at +0x42 into current HP at +0x40 and max MP at +0x46 into current MP at +0x44. Bit 0 of that status byte is the dead flag, so clearing the byte revives as well as heals. There is no side test and no retired test, and the sweep runs before the enemies are cleared, so it passes over the whole unit array and the character id is the only filter.
Four steps then run unconditionally. fdps_battle_destroy_remaining_enemies retires every enemy still standing on the battle map, so the victory scene plays over a cleared map. FUN_00023980 writes every active battle unit record back into the persistent roster table, resetting the per-battle fields as it goes; it keeps only bit 0 of the status byte (AND byte ptr [rec+0x5],0x1) and skips the restore of current HP from max for any record that still has that bit set, which is why the recovery sweep has to run ahead of it. FUN_00021650, the IconAni.vfs event-script interpreter, is handed the ASCIIZ resource name "Win23.dat" at 0x000621d0 -- the Win%02d.dat form named by the 0-based chapter index 23 -- and plays chapter 24's victory scene; the uint it returns is discarded. FUN_00039e70 then runs the paid revive over every party unit still at 0 HP, restoring it from its maximum and charging the per-class revive cost. Last, the chapter index global DAT_00069cf4 is set unconditionally to 0x18; that global is 0-based, so 0x18 selects the player's chapter 25, and it is the index every per-chapter handler table -- chapter init, post-action, chapter end -- is dispatched through afterwards.

Parameters:
  none -- main dispatches through the table at 0x00060304 with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup.

Returns:
  nothing; the effects are the conditional free full recovery of the twelve roster characters, the cleared map, the roster writeback, the victory scene it played, the paid revive pass and the advanced chapter index in DAT_00069cf4.

Pool: fdps  [reached only through the game's own chapter-end handler table; every callee is game code and the one data operand is the game resource name "Win23.dat"; Function ID matches no Watcom 10.0x or AIL library symbol and the body hash is unique in the image]

Rebuild note:
The recovery sweep has to stay ahead of FUN_00023980: that routine carries bit 0 of the unit status byte through into the roster and refuses to restore current HP from max for any record whose bit 0 is still set, so writing the order that reads more naturally -- bank the party, then heal it -- leaves the whole party recorded as dead going into chapter 25. Read the character id at +0x08 as an unsigned byte too: the original zero-extends it (MOV AL,[EAX+8] / AND EAX,0xff) before the <= 0x0b test, and Watcom's plain char is signed, so declaring that field char would let every id from 0x80 up pass the test and be healed.

=== 0003b6b0 [PLATE]

Algorithm:

Rebuild note:
Both stores to DAT_00069da0 are unconditional -- neither is wrapped in the "only while the code is still 0" guard that the shared end-condition check at 0003a2e0 puts around its own writes, and the defeat test runs after the victory test rather than as its else branch. Returns:

=== 0003b9f0 [PLATE]
Chapter 29's post-action handler: the win/lose test the battle loop runs after a unit has acted, reached through slot 28 of the per-chapter handler table based at 0x0006028c.

Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with an empty local area (PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP, MOV EBP,ESP, SUB ESP,0x0 in the 6-byte imm32 form), calls fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions and returns. That callee refreshes the chapter-event/battle-end code at DAT_00069da0 only while it is still 0: it presets 2 (chapter cleared), then walks unit indices 0..DAT_00060150-1 through fdps_get_unit_record and knocks the code back to 0 for as long as any record still has side byte +6 == 0 (the enemy side) with the retired bit -- bit 0 of byte +5 -- clear, so 2 survives only once no such unit is left; it then stores 1 (defeat), unguarded by whatever the sweep concluded, when fdps_unit_is_retired reports the chapter's protected unit gone -- unit 3 for chapter ids 0x10 and 0x15, and unit 0, Randis, for every other chapter, chapter 29 among them. Chapter 29 adds no condition of its own, matching the chapter's stated rules: win when every enemy is wiped out, lose when Randis dies. The slot exists as its own function rather than as a second pointer to fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions because every chapter owns a slot whether or not it has an extra condition; the chapter's own scripted business -- the right, lower-right and upper-middle enemy groups that break cover when the player crosses the line before the central junction, and the general attack that starts once a player unit reaches the upper room's entrance -- lives in fdps_chapter_29_event_activate_enemy_groups and fdps_chapter_29_event_activate_all_enemies, reached through slots 0x00060278 and 0x0006027c of the chapter-script event vector based at 0x000601c4, not from this postlude.

Parameters:

Returns:
  nothing; the outcome is left in DAT_00069da0, which the dispatch sites compare against 0 to decide whether to break out of the phase loop, and which main reads afterwards as 1 = defeat and 2 = chapter cleared, dispatching fdps_chapter_29_end out of the chapter-end table at 0x00060304 in the latter case.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the AIL set; the body's sole callee drives the unit record array and the chapter/battle-state globals, symbols no separately compiled vendor object could reference, and the frame plus plain RET is a compiled C body rather than a link-time jump island]

=== 0003ba50 [PLATE]
Chapter 30's post-action handler: the end-condition test the battle loop runs after a unit has acted, reached through slot 29 of the per-chapter handler table based at 0x0006028c.

Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with an empty local area, then calls fdps_unit_is_retired with unit index 0 -- Randis -- and, when it returns non-zero, stores 1 (defeat) into the chapter-event/battle-end code at DAT_00069da0. === 0003ba80 [PLATE]
Chapter 30's chapter-end handler, and with it the end of the game: clears the map, banks the party, plays chapter 30's victory scene, runs the ending sequence and the "GoodEnd.dat" epilogue, then asks the game to fall back to the title screen. Reached through slot 29, the last slot, of the chapter-end handler table based at 0x00060304.

Algorithm:
Builds the standard four-push Watcom frame with an empty local area, then runs six steps in order. fdps_battle_destroy_remaining_enemies wipes every enemy still standing on the battle map, so the scene plays over a cleared map. FUN_00023980 writes every active battle unit record back into the persistent roster table, resetting the per-battle fields as it goes. FUN_00021650, the IconAni.vfs event-script interpreter, is called with the ASCIIZ resource name "Win29.dat" and plays chapter 30's victory scene; its return value is discarded. Both DAT_00060158 and DAT_00060159 are then set to 1: they are the pair of gates fdps_draw_cursor_info_panel tests before drawing the battle-map cursor information panel -- 0x60158 is the player's own info-panel option, the fourth entry of fdps_options_menu and a field of the FDE.SAV image, and 0x60159 is the engine's suppression gate that menus, status windows and IconAni scenes drop while they cover the map -- so this raises both. FUN_0001ba40 runs the game's ending sequence: the Stand%03d.saf / Act%03d.saf / Back%02d.saf character gallery with its caption line, followed by the "End" movie. delay(30000) then holds for a flat thirty seconds with nothing polled. FUN_00021650 runs once more on "GoodEnd.dat" for the closing scene. Finally DAT_000643eb is set to 1: that is the return-to-title request flag main clears at 00029347 before it calls fdps_title_screen and that every phase loop tests -- fdps_run_village_phase bails out of its entry at 00031228 and again at 00031491 when it is set -- so raising it unwinds the battle and village phases and drops the game back on the title screen. Unlike every other handler in this table it writes no next chapter index into DAT_00069cf4, because there is no chapter 31.

Parameters:
  none -- the dispatch site calls through the handler table with nothing pushed and no stack cleanup.

Returns:
  nothing; the effects are the cleared map, the roster writeback, the three scenes it played, the two raised info-panel flags and the return-to-title request in DAT_000643eb.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the ail library set and the body hash is unique in the image; it calls only game routines plus the DOS clib delay, its data operands are the game resource names "Win29.dat" and "GoodEnd.dat", and it is reached only through the game's own chapter-end handler table]

Rebuild note:
This is the one chapter-end handler that must not follow the family pattern. Finishing it with a store of the next chapter index into DAT_00069cf4, the way every other slot of the table ends, sends the game into a chapter 31 that does not exist; the last chapter ends by raising the return-to-title flag DAT_000643eb instead. The pair of stores DAT_00060158 = 1 and DAT_00060159 = 1 is also not the save/restore idiom it resembles: 0x60158 is the player's persisted info-panel option and this handler forces it on without ever putting the old value back, so writing it as a save/restore around the ending sequence, or dropping it as redundant, changes what a player who had the panel switched off sees when a new game starts.

=== 0003bade [PLATE]
Allocates two 512-byte DOS real-mode buffers via DPMI INT 31h function 0100h and publishes their real-mode segments and flat linear addresses in the CD-ROM/MSCDEX globals.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; called only by fdps_cdrom_detect; writes the game's own CD state block]
Evidence: Link direction and shared data. The sole reference to the entry is the call from fdps_cdrom_detect at 0003c698, and its callees are the CRT helpers __CHK, memset and int386x - game code using the runtime, not runtime code. Function ID is empty against both the Watcom 10.0x libraries and ailv3.lib (0 candidates on each), so no vendor module owns these bytes. Every write lands in the 0x00069da4-0x00069e54 CD-ROM state area that fdps_cd_device_request reads; nothing touches CRT or AIL state. It is a full compiled body with a stack probe, so not binary_artifact.
Name: no library symbol identified; fdps_ + snake_case name describing what the body does, consistent with fdps_cdrom_detect and fdps_cd_device_request around it.
Boundary: 0003bade-0003bb7c, PUSH 0x14 / CALL __CHK is the Watcom stack-probe prologue at a real entry, the RET at 0003bb7c ends it, gap_after is empty, and 0003bb7d opens the identical prologue of fdps_cd_device_request.
Signature: void (void), __watcall. No argument register is read before being written and nothing is fetched from the caller's frame; each PUSH group is balanced by the function's own ADD ESP before a plain RET. For a zero-argument void function __watcall and __cdecl are indistinguishable in code, so __watcall is the compilation unit's default rather than a distinction the assembly makes.

Algorithm:
1. memset the 12-byte struct SREGS at 0x00069df0 to zero.
2. Fill the input REGS at 0x00069dc8 with AX = 0x0100 and BX = 0x0020, then call int386x(0x31, in, out, sregs). DPMI 0100h allocates 0x20 paragraphs (512 bytes) of DOS memory below 1MB; the returned AX is the real-mode segment and DX the protected-mode selector, which is discarded.
3. Store the first block's segment as a word at 0x00069e54 and its flat linear address (segment << 4) at 0x00069de8. DOS/4GW identity-maps the first megabyte, so segment << 4 is directly dereferenceable.
4. Repeat the identical DPMI 0100h call for a second 512-byte block; store its segment shifted left 16 bits at 0x00069da8 (a pre-packed seg:0000 real-mode far pointer for the MSCDEX request header's transfer address) and its flat linear address at 0x00069da4.

The input REGS block is not re-initialised before the second call because int386x leaves the caller's input structure untouched.

No error handling: a failed DPMI allocation returns with the carry flag set and garbage in AX, and the resulting addresses are used unchecked by the CD driver functions.

=== 0003bb7d [PLATE]
Sends the currently prepared MSCDEX request header to the CD-ROM device driver via real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h, issued through DPMI Simulate Real Mode Interrupt.
Pool: fdps  [no FID hit in either library set; game-owned CD state area at 0x00069dac-0x00069e54]
Evidence: All 13 callers are the CD-ROM cluster at 0003bce2-0003c6f9 (including fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and fdps_cd_stop_audio) and it shares their state block, so it is the game's own CD request primitive. Callees (memset, printf, int386x, __CHK) are generic CRT and identify nothing. Not AIL: no AIL module references it and it touches MSCDEX, not AIL state. Not crt: no runtime module builds MSCDEX headers against game globals. Not binary_artifact: full compiler-emitted body with a __CHK prologue.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code; no library symbol identified, and none can be (watcom and ail candidate counts are both 0).
Boundary: 0003bb7d-0003bc3e, entry is the PUSH 0x14 / CALL __CHK stack probe, body ends at the RET at 0003bc3e; gap_after is empty and 0003bc3f is the next function's own __CHK prologue.
Signature: void fdps_cd_device_request(void). No argument register or stack slot is read on entry and no value is returned; every input is a file-scope global (subunit number at 0x00069dfe, real-mode segment of the request header at 0x00069e54, the header itself). Callers fill the header before calling. __watcall and __cdecl are indistinguishable for a zero-argument void function.
Algorithm: clears the SREGS block at 0x00069df0 (12 bytes) and the DPMI real-mode call structure at 0x00069e22 (0x32 bytes); fills the real-mode structure with EAX=0x1510 (MSCDEX Send Device Request), ECX = the subunit byte at 0x00069dfe, EBX=0 and ES = the word at 0x00069e54, so the driver sees ES:BX pointing at the request header; then fills the protected-mode input REGS block at 0x00069dc8 with EAX=0x0300 (DPMI Simulate Real Mode Interrupt), BL=0x2f (the interrupt number, 2Fh), BH=0, CX=0 (no words copied from the stack) and EDI = 0x00069e22, sets SREGS.es to DS, and calls int386x(0x31, &in, &out, &sregs). If the output REGS carry flag at 0x00069dc4 is set it prints "DEVICE REQUEST FAILED!!!" and returns anyway; the MSCDEX status word inside the request header is not inspected here, so the caller must read it.

=== 0003bc3f [PLATE]
Splits a packed Red Book CD-ROM address (0x00MMSSFF) into its three separate byte fields, for callers that need minutes, seconds and frames one at a time.

Algorithm:
After the Watcom stack probe __CHK(4) the whole body is three byte stores taken straight out of the packed argument: the low byte of msf_packed to *frame, bits 8-15 to *second, bits 16-23 to *minute. Bits 24-31 are ignored. No globals are read or written and nothing is returned; the two callers own the results. FUN_0003bc78 turns them into a logical sector number (minute*4500 + second*75 + frame - 150, the 75-frames-per-second Red Book rate less the 150-frame pregap); fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info drops them into the CD lead-out globals DAT_00069e08 (minute), DAT_00069e09 (second) and DAT_00069e0a (frame).

Parameters:
  msf_packed -- packed Red Book address, 0x00MMSSFF, as the MSCDEX device driver reports track and lead-out positions; only the low 24 bits are used
  minute -- out; receives bits 16-23, the minutes field (0-99)
  second -- out; receives bits 8-15, the seconds field (0-59)
  frame -- out; receives bits 0-7, the frames field (0-74)

Returns:
  Nothing. The three results leave through the out-parameters.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; unique hash in image; called only by game CD-ROM code]

Rebuild note:
The parameter order is (packed, minute, second, frame) -- most-significant field first -- while the body stores least-significant field first; writing the call with the pointers in the order the stores appear, or in packed-bit order, silently swaps minutes and frames and the LBA computed from them is wrong by a factor of 4500. Nothing in the code range-checks the fields, so the swap does not fault, it just seeks to the wrong place on the disc.

=== 0003bc78 [PLATE]
Converts a packed Red Book CD-ROM address into the logical sector number of that position on the disc.

Algorithm:
Calls fdps_cd_unpack_msf to split the packed argument into its minute, second and frame bytes, written into three separate stack bytes. Then forms minute * 4500 + second * 75 + frame; both multiplies are open-coded shift/add chains, 4500 being 75 frames per second times 60 seconds per minute and 75 being frames per second. Finally subtracts 0x96 = 150 frames, the two-second lead-in that Red Book addressing places before logical sector 0, and returns the result.

Parameters:
  msf_packed -- a Red Book disc address packed as 0x00MMSSFF, minutes in bits 16-23, seconds in bits 8-15, frames in bits 0-7. fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info passes the lead-out address out of the MSCDEX disk-information reply; FUN_0003c0c8 passes the start address of the audio track it queried.

Returns:
  The logical sector number of that address, counted with 00:02:00 as sector 0. An address below 00:02:00 yields a negative value; neither caller checks for it.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; called only by game CD-ROM code]

Rebuild note:
The routine subtracts 150 frames before returning, so it yields a logical sector number and not the plain frame count of the address; writing the obvious minute*60*75 + second*75 + frame gives a value 150 too large, which would shift every CD-DA track start and the lead-out that fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and FUN_0003c0c8 publish. It also returns a signed value that goes negative for addresses under 00:02:00, and the callers rely on that not being clamped.

=== 0003bce2 [PLATE]
Reports where the CD-ROM drive's head is sitting, as a logical (HSG) sector number on the disc.

Algorithm:
Builds an MSCDEX IOCTL-input device request on the stack: header length 0x1e, subunit 0, command code 3 (IOCTL input), media descriptor 0, transfer address taken from DAT_00069da8 (the real-mode seg:0000 far pointer to the second DOS staging buffer), byte count 6, starting sector 0, volume-ID pointer 0. Only the 26 documented header bytes are filled in; the declared length is 0x1e and the four bytes past the documented end, along with the status and reserved fields, go to the driver as whatever was on the stack. Alongside it builds the 6-byte control block: byte 0 = 1 (location of head), byte 1 = 0 (HSG addressing, so the answer comes back as a sector number rather than minute/second/frame). memcpy puts the header into the DOS request buffer at DAT_00069de8 and the control block into the DOS transfer buffer at DAT_00069da4, then fdps_cd_device_request hands the packet to the CD-ROM device driver. Both blocks are copied back out of the DOS buffers -- the header for as many bytes as its own length field says, the control block for 6 -- the request status word at header+3 is published in DAT_00069e20, where fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy reads it, and the dword the driver wrote at control block +2 is returned.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  The location of the drive head as an HSG logical sector number. The call's success is not folded into the return value; a caller that needs it reads the status word left in DAT_00069e20.

Pool: fdps  [no FID hit in either library set, and it calls the game routine fdps_cd_device_request, which a library object could not do]

=== 0003bd99 [PLATE]
Reads the CD-ROM drive's audio channel routing and volume settings into the caller's 9-byte MSCDEX control block.

Algorithm:
Builds a 26-byte DOS device-driver request header in a 0x1c-byte stack buffer: length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3 (MSCDEX IOCTL Input), media descriptor 0, transfer address taken from the real-mode far pointer at DAT_00069da8, transfer count 9, starting sector 0, volume-ID pointer 0. The status word at header offset 3 and the eight reserved bytes at offsets 5..0x0c are deliberately left as they lie on the stack, since the driver overwrites the first and ignores the rest. Stamps control-block code 4 (Audio Channel Info) into channel_info[0], then memcpy's the header into the DOS-addressable request buffer whose flat linear address is in DAT_00069de8 and the 9-byte control block into the DOS-addressable control-block buffer whose flat linear address is in DAT_00069da4 -- the same DOS block DAT_00069da8 names as a real-mode segment, both published by fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers. Calls fdps_cd_device_request, which hands the packet to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. On return it copies the header back out of DAT_00069de8 (header[0] = 0x1a bytes), copies the nine answered control-block bytes back from DAT_00069da4 into channel_info, and latches the header's status word into DAT_00069e20. That last copy and the status latch are reached by a tail jump into the shared epilogue at 0x0003c590, which the function at 0x0003c51c also owns; in C it is straight-line code.

Parameters:
  channel_info -- pointer to a caller-owned 9-byte MSCDEX Audio Channel Info control block. The routine writes the function code into byte 0 itself; the driver fills bytes 1..8 with four (input channel, volume) pairs, one pair per output channel. The caller's bytes 1..8 are handed to the driver on the way in and are overwritten on the way out.

Returns:
  Nothing. Whether the request succeeded is reported only through the device request-header status word left in DAT_00069e20, where bit 15 is the driver's error flag.

Pool: fdps  [calls the game's own fdps_cd_device_request and shares the game's CD state block at 0x00069da4/0x00069da8/0x00069de8/0x00069e20; no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the AIL library set]

Rebuild note:
DAT_00069da4 and DAT_00069da8 are two views of the SAME DOS real-mode block: fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers writes the flat linear address (segment << 4) to 0x69da4 and the real-mode far pointer (segment << 16) to 0x69da8. This routine memcpy's through 0x69da4 but puts 0x69da8 into the request header's transfer-address field. Writing the obvious C -- one pointer for the buffer, used for both the copy and the header field -- breaks it either way round: the driver gets a far pointer it cannot resolve, or the memcpy writes to a protected-mode address that is not the buffer. The same split applies to every MSCDEX request builder in this family.

=== 0003be36 [PLATE]
Sets the CD-ROM drive's audio channel routing and volume, by issuing the MSCDEX IOCTL Output request whose control block code is 3 (Audio Channel Control).

Algorithm:
Stamps control block code 3 into byte 0 of the caller's 9-byte control_block; the eight bytes after it are the four (input channel, volume) pairs the caller already filled in for output channels 0 through 3. Builds a 24-byte DOS device driver request header in the stack frame: length 0x18 at offset 0, subunit 0 at 1, command 0x0c (IOCTL Output) at 2, media descriptor 0 at 0x0d, transfer address at 0x0e taken from DAT_00069da8, and byte count 9 at 0x12. The status word at offset 3 and the eight reserved bytes are left uninitialised; the driver fills the status in. Copies the header into the DOS request-header buffer at *DAT_00069de8 and the nine control bytes into the DOS control-block buffer at *DAT_00069da4 -- the pair of real-mode buffers fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers allocated, DAT_00069da8 being the same control-block buffer expressed as a real-mode seg:0000 far pointer for the driver, DAT_00069da4 its flat linear address for memcpy. Calls fdps_cd_device_request, which hands the header to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. Copies the header back out of *DAT_00069de8 over the stack copy, using the length byte at offset 0 as the count, and latches the returned status word (header offset 3) into DAT_00069e20, where fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy reads it. The nine control bytes are not copied back. The copy-back stretch from 0003bea0 on is shared code: fdps_cd_seek and fdps_cd_play_audio_range jump into it after pushing their own header length.

Parameters:
  control_block -- pointer to a writable 9-byte MSCDEX Audio Channel Control block. Byte 0 is overwritten with 3; bytes 1..8 are four (input channel, volume) pairs, one per output channel 0..3, each volume 0..0xff. Supplied by the caller; no caller exists in the image.

Returns:
  Nothing. The driver's verdict is left in the request-header status word copied to DAT_00069e20.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; calls the game's own fdps_cd_device_request and shares the CD transfer-buffer globals 00069da4 / 00069da8 / 00069de8 and the status global 00069e20 with the other MSCDEX packet builders]

Rebuild note:
The DOS control-block buffer is addressed through two different globals in the same function and they are not interchangeable: the request header's transfer-address field takes DAT_00069da8 (the buffer's real-mode segment shifted into the high half, i.e. a seg:0000 far pointer for the driver) while the memcpy that fills the buffer takes DAT_00069da4 (the same buffer's flat linear address). Writing the obvious C -- one pointer variable used for both -- either hands the driver a protected-mode address it cannot follow or memcpy's into linear address seg<<16, and in both cases the request goes out over uninitialised bytes with no error reported.

=== 0003bea0 [PLATE]
Pool: fdps
Shared epilogue of the MSCDEX/CD-ROM device request routines: takes the request-header length on the stack, copies the header back out of the real-mode request buffer at [0x00069de8] into the caller's 0x18-byte stack block via crt_memcpy, extracts the 16-bit MSCDEX status field at header+3 and stores it into the game global at 0x00069e20, then releases the caller's block and returns.
Evidence: Every path into this address comes from the game's CD-ROM driver glue, and every one of them is already judged fdps: FUN_0003c452 (Play Audio, command 0x84) and FUN_0003c3fa (Seek, command 0x83) each end with PUSH <len> / JMP 0x0003bea0, and FUN_0003be36 (IOCTL Output, command 0x0c) falls straight through into it after MOVZX EAX,[ESP] / PUSH EAX. All three build MSCDEX request packets and dispatch them through fdps_cd_device_request@0003bb7d. The work done here is the matching read-back half of that protocol: the word at request-header offset 3 is the MSCDEX status field, and it is stashed in a game global. That is application logic about a game-specific driver protocol, so crt is excluded -- no runtime routine knows the MSCDEX header layout. Not ail: nothing touches the .DIG driver structures or the 0x70000 sound state area. Not binary_artifact: it is not a thunk or jump island, it performs real work on game state; it is a compiler-outlined common epilogue whose instructions correspond directly to the tail of the game's own C source. The sole callee 0x000435bc is crt_memcpy (settled separately, CLIB3S.LIB Function ID hit), and a memcpy call says nothing about its caller's origin. No Function ID hit on this body at all.

=== 0003bec1 [PLATE]
Reads the CD's media catalog number (UPC) out of the CD-ROM drive and publishes it in the CD state globals.

Algorithm:
Builds a 0x1a-byte DOS device request header in the 0x28-byte stack frame -- length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3 (MSCDEX IOCTL Input), media descriptor 0, transfer address = the real-mode far pointer of the control-block buffer held in DAT_00069da8, transfer count 0x0b, starting sector 0, volume-ID pointer 0 -- and above it an 11-byte IOCTL control block whose byte 0 is 0x0e (UPC Code) and whose byte 1, the CONTROL/ADR byte, is preset to 2 (ADR = media catalog number). Header bytes 3..4 (status) and 5..0x0c (reserved) are left holding whatever was on the stack; the driver overwrites the first and ignores the rest. memcpy copies the header into the real-mode request buffer whose flat linear address is in DAT_00069de8, and the control block into the buffer whose flat linear address is in DAT_00069da4 -- the same DOS block DAT_00069da8 names as a real-mode far pointer, both published by fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers. fdps_cd_device_request then hands the packet to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. On return the control block is copied back from DAT_00069da4 and the header from DAT_00069de8 (0x1a bytes, the count taken from the local header's own length byte), the request header's status word at header offset 3 is latched into DAT_00069e20, and the CONTROL/ADR byte is tested: when the driver answered 0 there the disc carries no catalog number, and the block's 7-byte UPC/EAN field at block offset 2 is zeroed with memset. That 7-byte field is then copied into the global at DAT_00069e0f, which no other code in the image reads. The status word is recorded but never tested, so DAT_00069e0f is rewritten whether or not the driver accepted the request.

Parameters:
  None.

Returns:
  1, always; the value carries no information. What the routine produces is DAT_00069e0f (the 7-byte packed UPC/EAN, all zero when the disc has none) and DAT_00069e20 (the driver request's status word, bit 15 being the driver's error flag).

Pool: fdps  [calls the game's own fdps_cd_device_request and shares the CD state block at 0x00069da4/0x00069da8/0x00069de8/0x00069e20 with the neighbouring fdps_cdrom_* functions; no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the AIL library set]

Rebuild note:
The control block's CONTROL/ADR byte is deliberately preset to 2 before the request and tested against 0 after it, so the zero test fires only when the driver actively reports "no catalog number"; a rewrite that clears the whole control block first would blank DAT_00069e0f on every drive that leaves that byte alone. DAT_00069da4 and DAT_00069da8 are two views of the same DOS block -- flat linear address for the memcpy, real-mode far pointer for the header's transfer-address field -- and using one pointer for both breaks the request in one direction or the other.

=== 0003bfa5 [PLATE]
Reads the CD-ROM disk information summary (lowest/highest track and lead-out address) through the MSCDEX device driver. It builds a 26-byte device request header on the stack (length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3 = IOCTL Input, media descriptor 0, transfer address from 0x00069da8, byte count 7, sector 0) and a 7-byte IOCTL control block whose subcommand byte is 0x0A (Read Disk Info), copies both into the DOS-addressable staging buffers pointed to by 0x00069de8 and 0x00069da4, calls fdps_cd_device_request@0003bb7d, then copies both blocks back and distributes the reply: 6 payload bytes to 0x00069e16, lowest track to 0x00069e06, highest track to 0x00069e07, the lead-out address split into MSF at 0x00069e08/09/0a by 0003bc3f and converted to a frame/LBA count at 0x00069e0b by 0003bc78, and the request header status word from offset 3 to 0x00069e20.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; unique hash in the image]
Evidence: link direction in both directions. It calls fdps_cd_device_request@0003bb7d and the CD helpers 0003bc3f and 0003bc78, all of which are game code, and a linked library object cannot reference the game's own symbols; its four static callers (fdps_cdrom_detect@0003c636, 0003c1a1, 0003c27c, 0003c8e6) are game code too, and 0003c636 is reached from main. It writes the game's CD-ROM globals at 0x69e06..0x69e20 and shares the low-memory staging pointers with the rest of the CD module. memcpy, memset and __CHK are CRT callees, which is the normal direction and not evidence against fdps. Every reference to this address is a direct call, so no pointer table dispatches it. 291 bytes of real logic rules out binary_artifact; nothing touches AIL structures.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code; confirmed by the IOCTL subcommand byte 0x0A (Read Disk Info) and the track/lead-out fields the body unpacks. No library symbol involved, and no other address claims the symbol.
Boundary: 0003bfa5-0003c0c7, own __CHK prologue at the start, balancing ADD ESP,0x24 / RET at the end, zero gap before the next function's identical prologue at 0003c0c8.
Signature: void (void). No register or stack argument is read and no call site passes one. The return is void on the callers' own evidence: all four discard EAX at once, and 0003c636 re-reads the status word from DAT_00069e20 rather than from the register the function left it in. Stack convention (__cdecl), the binary's -4s default, with no deviation signal present: this unit calls its game helpers with pushed arguments and caller cleanup (ADD ESP,0x10 / ADD ESP,4), and both helpers are themselves __cdecl.

=== 0003c0c8 [PLATE]
Reads the MSCDEX Audio Track Info block for one CD-ROM track and publishes that track's start position and control field in the CD state globals.

Algorithm:
Builds a 0x1a-byte DOS device request header on the stack -- length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3 (IOCTL Input), media descriptor 0, transfer address = the real-mode far pointer of the control-block buffer held in DAT_00069da8, transfer count 7, starting sector 0, volume ID pointer 0 -- together with a 7-byte IOCTL control block whose byte 0 is 0x0b (Read Audio Track Info) and whose byte 1 is the low byte of track. memcpy copies the header into the real-mode request buffer at DAT_00069de8 and the control block into the buffer at DAT_00069da4; fdps_cd_device_request hands the request to the CD-ROM device driver; memcpy copies both blocks back. The reply is then unpacked into the CD state globals: the request header's status word (header offset 3) into DAT_00069e20, the control block's packed Red Book start address (block offset 2) through fdps_cd_msf_to_sector into DAT_00069e01 as a logical sector number, the caller's track number into DAT_00069dff, and the control block's track control byte (block offset 6) masked with 0xd0 into DAT_00069e05. The 0xd0 mask keeps the ADR/control bits that distinguish data from audio and mark four-channel audio and drops the copy-permitted bit; fdps_cd_track_is_audio compares the stored value against 0x40. The status word is recorded but never tested here, so the track globals are overwritten whether or not the driver accepted the request. Bytes 5..12 of the header (the reserved area) are left holding whatever was on the stack.

Parameters:
  track -- CD-ROM track number to query; 1 through the highest track number on the disc, which fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info leaves in DAT_00069e07. Callers pass a zero-extended byte or a sign-extended 16-bit track number. Only the low byte reaches the driver; the low 16 bits reach DAT_00069dff.

Returns:
  Nothing. The results are the globals DAT_00069dff (the track just queried), DAT_00069e01 (its start sector), DAT_00069e05 (its masked control byte) and DAT_00069e20 (the driver request's status word).

Pool: fdps  [builds MSCDEX device request packets by hand; no Function ID match, watcom and ail candidate counts both 0]

Rebuild note:
The track control byte is masked with 0xd0, not the 0xf0 that the obvious 'take the control nibble' rewrite would use. 0x20 is the copy-permitted bit, and fdps_cd_track_is_audio decides audio-vs-data by comparing the stored value against 0x40 exactly; masking with 0xf0 would make every audio track that permits copying read back as 0x60 and be reported as a data track, so the game would refuse to play it.

=== 0003c1a1 [PLATE]
Reports the playing length of one CD audio track as a count of CD frames (sectors).

Algorithm:
Refreshes the disc summary with fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which republishes the disc's highest track number in the byte at 00069e07 and its lead-out sector in 00069e0b. Saves the track number that the CD track-info globals currently describe, from the word at 00069dff. Calls FUN_0003c0c8 (MSCDEX Read Audio Track Info) for the requested track and takes that track's start sector from 00069e01. When track is below the highest track number at 00069e07, compared unsigned, it queries track + 1 the same way and uses that track's start sector as the end point; when track is the last track on the disc it uses the lead-out sector at 00069e0b instead. It then calls FUN_0003c0c8 once more with the track number saved on entry, so the shared track-info globals 00069dff, 00069e01 and 00069e05 are left describing the same track they described before the call. Finally it returns end sector minus start sector. Both sector numbers come out of fdps_cd_msf_to_sector, which subtracts the 150-frame (2-second) lead-in, so that offset cancels in the subtraction and the result is a plain frame count at 75 frames per second.

Parameters:
  track -- CD-ROM track number, from the disc's lowest track at 00069e06 to its highest at 00069e07. Only the low byte of the argument slot is read. fdps_cd_get_track_length_msf passes its own track parameter through unchanged.

Returns:
  The track's length in CD frames: the number of sectors between the start of this track and the start of the next one, or between the start of the last track and the disc's lead-out.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library; calls fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and shares the disc-info globals the game's own CD-ROM layer owns]

Rebuild note:
The final FUN_0003c0c8 call at 0003c205 is not redundant: it re-queries the track that was selected on entry so that the shared track-info globals (00069dff track number, 00069e01 start sector, 00069e05 control byte) are restored, and fdps_cd_resolve_track_range reads exactly those globals to decide which track's range to publish. Writing the obvious C -- query this track, query the next, return the difference -- drops that restoring call and leaves the CD layer pointing at the wrong track, so a following play/seek can address the next track instead of the current one.

=== 0003c217 [PLATE]
Reports the playing time of one CD audio track as a Red Book minute/second/frame triple.

Algorithm:
Calls fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors for the length of the requested track in CD frames -- that routine returns the difference between the next track's start sector and this track's, or between the lead-out sector at DAT_00069e0b and this track's start when the track is the last one. Subtracts 0x96 = 150 frames, the two-second lead-in pre-gap, from that length; see the note below, the value it subtracts from carries no pre-gap term. Divides the result by 0x4b = 75, the number of frames in one CD second: the remainder is stored through frames and the quotient is the whole number of seconds. Divides that by 0x3c = 60: the remainder is stored through seconds and the quotient through minutes. Each division is written as (value - remainder) / divisor rather than as a bare quotient, so the same quotient is computed twice. All three divisions are unsigned (DIV, never IDIV) and all three results are stored as single bytes. Nothing is returned and no global is touched here; fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors refreshes the disc-info globals at 00069dff-00069e0b as a side effect of the query and puts the previously selected track back afterwards.

Parameters:
  track -- audio track number on the disc, 1..the highest-track byte at DAT_00069e07; passed straight through to fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors
  minutes -- out: whole minutes of the track's playing time
  seconds -- out: seconds within the minute, 0..59
  frames -- out: frames (sectors) within the second, 0..74

Returns:
Nothing. The three results leave through the out-pointers.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; the only real callee, fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, is game code that reaches fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and the game's own MSCDEX disc-info globals, and Red Book track timing is not a CLIB3S, MATH387S or AIL service]

Note: the 150-frame subtraction is applied to a duration, not to an absolute Red Book address, so it takes off two seconds that are not there. fdps_cd_msf_to_sector (0003bc78) already ends on SUB EAX,0x96 when it converts a packed Red Book address into a sector number, and every value in the disc-info globals passes through it, so the difference fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors returns has no pre-gap term left and this routine reports every track two seconds short. The subtraction is the module's fixed convention rather than an adjustment chosen for track lengths: the identical SUB 0x96 opens the same /75, /60 chain in fdps_cd_sector_to_msf, which receives its input as a plain sector argument and so cannot be encoding anything about tracks, and in fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf, which applies it to the absolute lead-out sector. None of the three has a caller or a data reference anywhere in the image, so the short value never reaches the player.

Rebuild note:
The routine subtracts 150 frames from a value that is already a duration: fdps_cd_msf_to_sector removes the two-second pre-gap when it converts each Red Book address into a sector number, so the difference fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors returns has no pre-gap term left and every track comes out two seconds short. Writing the obvious duration conversion -- frames/75 and /60 with no subtraction -- gives a different answer, so the 0x96 must be kept. The divisions are also unsigned: for a length below 150 frames the subtraction wraps and the triple becomes a huge value, where signed C int arithmetic would give a small negative one, so the intermediate must be an unsigned type. The same pre-gap convention is inlined in fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf and stands alone in fdps_cd_sector_to_msf, so all three must be reproduced the same way.

=== 0003c27c [PLATE]
Reports the two facts the game can want about the CD as a whole: the highest track number on the disc, and the disc's total playing time as a Red Book minute/second/frame triple.

Algorithm:
Calls fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues the MSCDEX Read Disk Info IOCTL and republishes the answer in the CD globals, so the values used below are always freshly read from the drive. Copies the highest-track byte DAT_00069e07 out through highest_track_out. Then takes the lead-out sector count DAT_00069e0b and subtracts 0x96 (150 sectors, the two seconds of lead-in that Red Book addressing counts before track 1) to get the playing length in sectors, and splits that unsigned value into the triple: remainder modulo 0x4b (75 sectors, one second of CD audio) is the frames field, the quotient's remainder modulo 0x3c (60) is the seconds field, and the final quotient is the minutes field. Each of the three is stored as a single byte through its pointer.

Parameters:
  highest_track_out -- where to store the number of the last track on the disc, taken from the disk-info block's highest-track byte; 1..99 on a Red Book disc. Written first, before the time conversion.
  minutes_out -- where to store the minutes field of the total playing time.
  seconds_out -- where to store the seconds field, 0..59.
  frames_out -- where to store the frames field, 0..74; one frame is 1/75 second.

Returns:
Nothing. All four results come back through the caller's pointers.

Pool: fdps  [calls fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and reads the CD globals that routine fills; no Function ID hit in any library, and a compiled vendor object could not call a symbol defined in the game's own source]

=== 0003c2e8 [PLATE]
Converts a CD sector count into a minute/second/frame triple, writing the three fields as separate bytes through caller-supplied pointers. The inverse of fdps_cd_msf_to_sector.

Algorithm:
Subtracts 0x96 (150 frames, the two-second lead-in pregap) from sector, then decomposes what is left with unsigned 32-bit divisions: value % 0x4b (75 frames per second) is stored through frame, (value - frame) / 0x4b is the total second count, that count % 0x3c (60 seconds per minute) is stored through second, and (count - second) / 0x3c is stored through minute. Each division is written as (value - remainder) / divisor rather than as a bare quotient, which is why the same quotient is computed twice; the first divisor is spilled to a stack local and read back by DIV dword ptr [ESP]. Calls __CHK(0x10) on entry for the Watcom stack probe, reads no global and writes none.

sector is a count in the unit the whole CD module uses: the pregap-corrected number fdps_cd_msf_to_sector returns, which fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info stores in DAT_00069e0b and fdps_cdrom_read_track_info stores in DAT_00069e01. The 0x96 is therefore taken off a second time and the triple comes out two seconds earlier than a plain decomposition of the same count would give. That is the module's uniform convention, not a quirk of this routine: fdps_cd_get_track_length_msf and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf inline the identical arithmetic, over a track length and over the lead-out sector, and subtract 0x96 the same way.

No call site in the image reaches this entry and no data reference points at it.

Parameters:
  sector -- unsigned CD frame (sector) count to convert. Values below 0x96 wrap the unsigned subtraction and yield a meaningless triple; nothing in the body guards against it.
  minute -- out: receives the minute field.
  second -- out: receives the second field, 0-59.
  frame -- out: receives the frame field, 0-74.

Returns:
  Nothing. All three results leave through the pointers.

Pool: fdps  [no library match; a member of the game's MSCDEX/CD-DA object, whose other members call fdps_cd_device_request and fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and share the CD state globals at 00069da4-00069e54, so the block is the game's own source]

Rebuild note:
The pregap is subtracted, not added, and it is subtracted from a value that has already had it taken off. The textbook conversion decomposes sector + 150; the plain duration conversion decomposes sector with no adjustment at all; this routine decomposes sector - 150, because its input is the pregap-corrected count fdps_cd_msf_to_sector produces. Writing either obvious formula shifts every result by two or four seconds against the original, so the 0x96 must be kept exactly where it is. sector must also stay unsigned: the subtraction and all four divisions are unsigned 32-bit (SUB then DIV, never IDIV), so an input below 150 wraps to a huge frame count instead of going negative, and declaring the parameter int changes what the divisions produce in exactly that case. The same convention is inlined in fdps_cd_get_track_length_msf and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf, so all three must be reproduced the same way.

=== 0003c34f [PLATE]
Reads the CD-ROM drive's device status from MSCDEX, leaving both the driver's device status dword and the status word of the request that carried it in the CD globals.

Algorithm:
Builds a 0x1a-byte MSCDEX device request header in the stack frame: header length 0x1a, subunit 0, command code 3 (IOCTL Input), media descriptor 0, transfer address = the real-mode segment:offset of the CD data buffer held in DAT_00069da8, transfer byte count 5, starting sector 0, volume id pointer 0. Beside it it lays out the 5-byte IOCTL Input control block, setting only its first byte to control block code 6 (Device Status); the four bytes behind it are left as they lie, since the driver is the one that fills them. memcpy copies the header into the real-mode request buffer at the linear address in DAT_00069de8 and the control block into the data buffer at the linear address in DAT_00069da4, then fdps_cd_device_request hands the packet to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. Two more memcpy calls read both buffers back into the stack copies. The four device status bytes the driver returned at control block offset 1 are stored in DAT_00069e1c. The body then falls into the tail at 0x0003c0ba, an epilogue Watcom merged with fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which stores the request header's status word (header offset 3) into DAT_00069e20 -- the word whose BUSY bit (0x0200) fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy tests.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  Nothing. Both results leave through globals: DAT_00069e1c takes the MSCDEX device status dword, DAT_00069e20 the request header status word.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; it calls fdps_cd_device_request and is called by fdps_cd_audio_is_idle, and shares the CD state globals 0x00069da4 / 0x00069da8 / 0x00069de8 with the rest of the CD subsystem]

Rebuild note:
The body's last instruction is JMP 0x0003c0ba, an epilogue Watcom merged with fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, and that shared tail is part of this function's C source: it stores the request header's status word into DAT_00069e20. Rewriting the function from the listing and stopping at the store to DAT_00069e1c drops that store, and since fdps_cd_audio_is_idle ignores everything this function publishes except that one global's BUSY bit, the idle test would then answer from whatever the previous CD request left behind and the game would stop waiting correctly for CD audio to finish.

=== 0003c3fa [PLATE]
Issues an MSCDEX Seek to the CD-ROM drive, moving the drive head to one logical sector without transferring any data.

Algorithm:
Builds a 24-byte MSCDEX device request header in a stack local: length 0x18 at offset 0, subunit 0 at offset 1, command code 0x83 (Seek) at offset 2, addressing mode 0 (HSG logical sector) at offset 0x0d, transfer address 0 at offset 0x0e, sector count 0 at offset 0x12, and the caller's sector at offset 0x14 (the request's starting sector number). Offsets 3 to 0x0c -- the status word and the eight reserved bytes -- are left as they lie; the driver fills the status. memcpy copies the 0x18 bytes into the DOS real-mode transfer buffer whose linear address is held in DAT_00069de8, then fdps_cd_device_request hands the request to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. The routine finishes through the shared epilogue at 0003bea0, reached by a tail JMP with the header size 0x18 already pushed as the memcpy count; that epilogue is the cross-jumped tail of FUN_0003be36 and copies the header back out of the transfer buffer, stores the driver's status word from header offset 3 into DAT_00069e20, drops the 0x18-byte frame and returns. DAT_00069e20 is the status word fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy and fdps_cd_audio_is_idle test.

Parameters:
  sector -- HSG logical sector to seek to, counted from the start of the disc; the units fdps_cd_msf_to_sector produces (minutes*4500 + seconds*75 + frames - 150). Nothing in the image calls this routine, so no caller pins the value further.

Returns:
  Nothing. The driver's status reaches the caller only through DAT_00069e20; the EAX left by the shared epilogue is the raw dword read at header offset 3 and is not a result.

Pool: fdps  [no FID candidate in either library set; calls the game routine fdps_cd_device_request and shares the CD transfer-buffer global DAT_00069de8 with the rest of the game's MSCDEX wrappers]

=== 0003c452 [PLATE]
Issues the MSCDEX Play Audio request that starts CD-DA playback over one range of disc sectors.

Algorithm:
Builds a 22-byte (0x16) MSCDEX device request header in a 0x18-byte stack frame: header length 0x16 at +0, subunit 0 at +1, command code 0x84 (Play Audio) at +2, addressing mode 0 (HSG / logical sector) at +0x0d, start_sector as a dword at +0x0e, and the sector count end_sector - start_sector as a dword at +0x12. The status word and reserved area at +3..+0x0c are not written; the driver fills them in. memcpy copies the packet into the real-mode transfer buffer whose flat address is held in DAT_00069de8, then fdps_cd_device_request hands it to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. The routine finishes by pushing the header length 0x16 and tail-jumping to the shared CD request epilogue at 0x0003bea0 (the merged tail inside FUN_0003be36), which copies the packet back out of the transfer buffer, records the driver's status word in DAT_00069e20 and releases the 0x18-byte frame. Playback is asynchronous: the request completes as soon as the driver accepts it, and fdps_cd_audio_is_idle reports when the range has finished playing.

Parameters:
  start_sector -- first disc sector to play, as a logical (HSG) sector number. fdps_cd_play_track passes DAT_00069dec, the track start published by fdps_cd_resolve_track_range.
  end_sector -- one past the last sector to play; the packet carries end_sector - start_sector as its sector count. Callers pass DAT_00069de4, the start of the following track or the disc's lead-out address.

Returns:
  Nothing. The driver's status word is left in DAT_00069e20 by the shared epilogue, and both callers discard whatever the epilogue leaves in EAX.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit; it builds the game's own MSCDEX request packets and shares the request-buffer pointer DAT_00069de8 with the neighbouring fdps_cd_* wrappers]

Rebuild note:
The sector-count field at packet offset +0x12 is written as a full dword (MOV dword ptr [ESP+0x12],EAX at 0003c482), which is what makes the header exactly 0x16 bytes long; Ghidra's decompilation renders it as a 16-bit store (local_6 = (undefined2)(end_sector - start_sector)). Emitting the obvious C from that decompilation gives a 2-byte count with two bytes of uninitialised stack garbage above it, so the driver is asked to play a wildly wrong number of sectors. The count must be a 32-bit field.

=== 0003c4a7 [PLATE]
Stop CD audio playback: builds a 13-byte MSCDEX device request header with command code 0x85 (Stop Audio), copies it into the real-mode transfer buffer at *DAT_00069de8, issues the driver request, copies the reply back and stores the returned status word into DAT_00069e20.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit; sole substantive callee and every caller are game code]
Evidence: Calls fdps_cd_device_request@0003bb7d and is called only by named game code (main, fdps_title_screen, fdps_play_movie, fdps_cd_play_track, fdps_cd_verify_disc_and_play_track and neighbouring CD wrappers); a CRT or AIL module could not reference game-defined symbols. Name: No library symbol; named from the packet it assembles - header length 0x0D, subunit 0, command code 0x85 = MSCDEX Stop Audio, with the adjacent 0003c4ff emitting the same shape with command 0x88 = Resume Audio.
Boundary: 0003c4a7-0003c4fe, entry is the Watcom PUSH 0x20 / CALL __CHK stack probe that every caller targets, and the RET at 0003c4fe follows the ADD ESP,0x10 that unwinds the frame; gap_after is empty and 0003c4ff starts its own identical preamble.
Signature: __watcall, no arguments, void return. No incoming register or stack slot is read before being written, stack purge is 0, and EAX at the end only carries the status word into the global rather than out to the caller.

=== 0003c4ff [PLATE]
Resumes CD-DA playback that was halted earlier, by issuing the MSCDEX Resume Audio Play command to the CD-ROM device driver.

Algorithm:
  Probes 0x20 bytes of stack through __CHK, then opens a 0x10-byte frame that holds a 13-byte MSCDEX device request header. It fills three header fields and nothing else: byte 0 = 0x0d (header length), byte 1 = 0x00 (subunit), byte 2 = 0x88 (Resume Audio Play command code); the status word at +3 and the reserved bytes from +5 are left holding whatever was in the frame, which is what the driver expects for this command.
  It then jumps to 0003c4c2, the epilogue it shares with fdps_cd_stop_audio -- the two routines are identical apart from the command byte (0x88 here, 0x85 Stop Audio there) and the compiler tail-merged them. That shared trailer memcpy's the 13-byte header into the real-mode transfer buffer whose flat address is held in DAT_00069de8, calls fdps_cd_device_request to hand the request to the driver via real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h, memcpy's the 13 bytes back out of the transfer buffer, stores the header's status word (offset +3) into DAT_00069e20, releases the frame and returns.

Parameters:
  none.

Returns:
  nothing. The driver's reply is published in the CD status global DAT_00069e20, where fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy reads it.

Pool: fdps  [game CD-audio code; no Function ID hit in either library set]

=== 0003c51c [PLATE]
Issues one MSCDEX IOCTL Output request whose control block is a single command byte, for the drive commands that carry no data of their own.

Algorithm:
Builds a 0x18-byte DOS device-driver request header in a stack local: header length 0x18, subunit 0, command code 0x0c (IOCTL Output), media descriptor 0, transfer address = the real-mode segment:offset of the IOCTL control-block buffer held in DAT_00069da8, transfer byte count 1. The status word at header+3 and the eight reserved bytes are left as they lie; the driver fills the status in. Stores command_code into a one-byte stack local, then memcpy's the header into the real-mode request-header buffer at DAT_00069de8 and that one byte into the real-mode control-block buffer at DAT_00069da4. Calls fdps_cd_device_request, which hands the header to MSCDEX through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. memcpy's the 0x18 header bytes back out of DAT_00069de8 and stores the returned status word (header+3) into DAT_00069e20, the global that fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy reads.

Everything from the control-block copy onward is a tail shared with fdps_cd_set_door_lock: that function builds its own two-byte control block, pushes a count of 2 and jumps to 0x0003c56b.

Parameters:
  command_code -- MSCDEX IOCTL Output control block code, used as a byte. fdps_cd_close_tray passes 5 (Close Tray); the same request shape also carries 0 (Eject Disk) and 2 (Reset Drive).

Returns:
  Nothing. The outcome is the driver's request-header status word, left in DAT_00069e20.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit on either library set; calls fdps_cd_device_request, a function of the game's own source]

=== 0003c56b [PLATE]
Pool: fdps
Builds a CD-ROM device request on the stack from a global template, issues it via fdps_cd_device_request, then copies a 0x18-byte reply block from a global buffer back onto the stack and stores a word of the result into the global at 0x00069e20.
Evidence: Disassembly is a thin game-side wrapper around the already-named fdps_cd_device_request at 0003bb7d, using two copy calls to FUN_000435bc (memcpy-shaped: dest, src, 0x18) and three FDPS globals (0x00069da4, 0x00069de8, 0x00069e20). No Function ID hits against CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387, and no CRT idiom (no errno, no heap/stdio/FPU work) -- a runtime routine would not call a game CD-request helper. Not AIL: no interrupt path, no .DIG driver structures, no 0x70000 state area; the CD access here is the game's own MSCDEX-style request plumbing, and its only caller is game code FUN_0003c7aa.
