=== 0003c5a6 [PLATE]
Fetches the CD-ROM drive's audio Q-channel into a caller-supplied 11-byte control block, so the caller can see which track is playing and how far into that track the drive has got.

Algorithm:
Writes MSCDEX IOCTL-input control code 0x0c (Audio Q-Channel Info) into q_channel[0], then builds a 26-byte DOS device request header on the stack: length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3 (IOCTL input), media descriptor 0, transfer address = the real-mode seg:0000 far pointer of the CD control-block buffer published in DAT_00069da8 by fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers, byte count 6, starting sector 0, volume-ID pointer 0. The status word and the eight reserved bytes are left holding whatever was on the stack. memcpy copies the header into the DOS request buffer at [DAT_00069de8] and the 11-byte control block into the DOS transfer buffer at [DAT_00069da4], and fdps_cd_device_request hands the header to the CD-ROM device driver through real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h. Both buffers are then copied back -- 0x1a header bytes and 0x0b control-block bytes -- and the header's status word at header+3 is stored in DAT_00069e20, the saved request status that fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy tests.
The control-block copy-back, the status store and the RET are not in this function's own bytes: the body ends in a tail JMP to LAB_0003be27, the epilogue of FUN_0003bd99, which jumps on into LAB_0003c590 in FUN_0003c51c and returns from there. The three routines build the same request header with different control codes and share one epilogue.
On return q_channel holds the driver's Q-channel reply; the caller reads +2 as the track now playing and +4/+5/+6 as the minute, second and frame reached within that track.

Parameters:
  q_channel -- pointer to an 11-byte MSCDEX audio Q-channel control block owned by the caller. Byte 0 is overwritten with the control code; the rest comes back filled by the driver. fdps_cd_read_audio_position, the only caller, passes the game's fixed block at DAT_00069e56.

Returns:
  Nothing. The results are the filled q_channel block and the request status word left in DAT_00069e20.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; it calls fdps_cd_device_request and writes the CD real-mode buffer globals, which a third-party library object could not reference]

Rebuild note:
The request header asks for a 6-byte transfer while the control block it points at is 11 bytes, and the caller reads the frame field at offset 6 -- one byte past the declared count. Writing the obvious C, i.e. setting the byte count to sizeof the Q-channel block (11) or to the 0x0b both memcpy's use, changes what the game asks the CD driver for; keep the literal 6.

=== 0003c636 [PLATE]

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom libraries or ailv3.lib; calls game code and shares the CD state area]
Evidence: Calls fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers (0003bade) and fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info (0003bfa5) and is called only by main@00029220 - a linked library object cannot reference the game's own symbols. === 0003c6bc [PLATE]
Closes the CD-ROM drive tray and reports whether the drive came back not busy.

Algorithm:
Probes 8 bytes of stack through the Watcom __CHK stub, then calls the MSCDEX IOCTL-Output request builder fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command with control block code 5, which is Close Tray in the MSCDEX IOCTL Output control block table, and cleans that one stacked argument off with ADD ESP,4. The body has no RET of its own: it ends at 0003c6cf and runs straight on into fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy at 0003c6d0, which supplies the return value by testing bit 0x0200 -- the DOS device-driver request-header BUSY bit -- of the status word fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command latched into DAT_00069e20. That run-on is this routine's tail call to the predicate, with the JMP dropped because the target happens to be the next function; fdps_cd_audio_is_idle makes the same tail call from further away and still carries an explicit JMP 0003c6d0.

Nothing in the image calls this entry or references its address. That is the norm for this CD layer rather than a sign of misidentification: most of its entry points are equally unreferenced and the module survives because it was linked whole.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  ushort -- 1 when the BUSY bit of the status word that the Close Tray request left in DAT_00069e20 is clear, 0 when it is still set.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit on either library set; its only real callee is game code that marshals MSCDEX device requests, which a third-party library object could not reference]

Rebuild note:
This function has no RET of its own -- the 20 bytes at 0003c6bc end in ADD ESP,4 and run into the predicate at 0003c6d0. Emitting only what Ghidra shows inside the body gives void fdps_cd_close_tray(void) { fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command(5); }, which silently drops the 0/1 status the original hands back. The rebuilt source must end in that value: either return fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy(); -- the reading fdps_cd_audio_is_idle's explicit tail JMP to the same address supports -- or the DAT_00069e20 BUSY-bit test written out again. Both are functionally equivalent; a void body is not.

=== 0003c6d0 [PLATE]
Predicate on the CD-ROM driver's last request: returns 1 when the BUSY bit of the saved MSCDEX request-header status word is clear.

Algorithm:
Loads the 16-bit status word that the CD request routines saved at DAT_00069e20, masks it down to bit 9 alone (XOR AL,AL drops the error-code byte, AND AH,0x2 keeps 0x0200, the BUSY bit of the DOS device-driver request-header status word), and returns SETZ of that mask: 1 when the bit is clear, 0 when it is set. It touches no other memory and calls nothing.

The body is also the shared tail of the two routines that lead into it, both of which end with this same test in their C source. FUN_0003c6bc issues its IOCTL Output request through FUN_0003c51c and then falls straight through at 0003c6cf, having no RET of its own; fdps_cd_audio_is_idle calls FUN_0003c34f for the device-status IOCTL and tail-jumps here at 0003c6f7. DAT_00069e20 itself is written by FUN_0003c51c at 0003c59c and on the path out of FUN_0003c34f, in each case from the request header copied back out of the real-mode transfer buffer at DAT_00069de8 after fdps_cd_device_request.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  1 when the saved status word's BUSY bit (0x0200) is clear -- the driver reports no request or audio playback in progress -- and 0 when it is set.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit on either the Watcom or the AIL set, and the one datum it touches is the CD status global that the game's own CD layer writes]

=== 0003c6e8 [PLATE]
Asks MSCDEX for the CD-ROM device status and returns 1 when the driver request's BUSY bit is clear, i.e. audio playback has finished.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in any vendor library; game CD-audio glue]

=== 0003c6f9 [PLATE]
Asks the CD-ROM driver whether the disc has been swapped since the last time it was asked, and hands back MSCDEX's media-change byte.

Algorithm:
Builds a 26-byte MSCDEX device request header in its 0x20-byte stack frame: length 0x1a, subunit 0, command code 3 (IOCTL Input), media descriptor 0 at +0x0d, transfer address at +0x0e taken from DAT_00069da8 (the real-mode seg:off of the control-block buffer), byte count 2 at +0x12, sector count 0 at +0x14 and start sector 0 at +0x16. Beside the header, at frame+0x1c, it builds the 2-byte IOCTL Input control block whose first byte is subcommand 9, Media Changed; the second byte is the driver's answer and is not initialised on the way out. memcpy copies the header into the real-mode request buffer at DAT_00069de8 and the control block into the real-mode data buffer at DAT_00069da4, fdps_cd_device_request issues the driver call, and two further memcpy calls copy both blocks back out of those buffers. The header's returned status word (header+3) is then stored into DAT_00069e20 -- the same global fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy tests for the BUSY bit -- and the control block's answer byte is returned.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  The MSCDEX media-change byte, zero-extended into AX: 1 means the disc has not been changed, 0 means the driver cannot tell, 0xff means the disc has been changed. It is not a boolean and it is not a 0/1 predicate. The upper half of EAX still holds header bytes 5 and 6 left over from the status-word load and carries no meaning.

Pool: fdps  [calls the game function fdps_cd_device_request, which a compiled library object could not; no Function ID hit in the Watcom or ail sets]

Rebuild note:
The returned byte is MSCDEX's tri-state media-change value, where 1 means the disc has NOT changed, 0 means unknown and 0xff means it has changed -- writing the obvious 'return changed != 0;' or treating the result as a boolean inverts the common case. Separately, the epilogue is MOV EAX,dword ptr [ESP+0x3] followed by a 16-bit MOVZX AX,byte ptr [ESP+0x1d], so only AX is meaningful and the top half of EAX still holds request-header bytes 5 and 6; the return type must stay a 16-bit type or a rewrite will hand callers a cleanly zero-extended EAX the original never produced.

=== 0003c7aa [PLATE]
Locks or unlocks the CD-ROM drive door, so the disc cannot be swapped while the game is using it.

Algorithm:
Builds a 0x18-byte MSCDEX device-driver request header in a 0x1c-byte stack frame: byte 0 = header length 0x18, byte 1 = subunit 0, byte 2 = command 0x0c (IOCTL Output), byte 0x0d = media descriptor 0, dword 0x0e = the real-mode address of the control-block transfer buffer taken from DAT_00069da8, word 0x12 = transfer length 2. Directly behind the header, at frame offset 0x18, it lays down the 2-byte IOCTL Output control block { 0x01 = Lock/Unlock Door, lock }. memcpy copies the 0x18-byte header into the real-mode request buffer whose flat address is held in DAT_00069de8; the routine then pushes the control-block length 2 and jumps to 0x0003c56b, the shared request tail it has in common with FUN_0003c51c. That tail memcpys the control block into the real-mode transfer buffer at DAT_00069da4, calls fdps_cd_device_request to hand the request to the CD-ROM driver, copies the header back out of DAT_00069de8, latches its status word (header offset 3) into DAT_00069e20 -- which is what fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy reads -- and returns.
The header fields this routine never writes (the status word at +3, the reserved bytes 5..0x0c, the start sector at +0x14 and the volume-ID pointer at +0x16) reach the driver holding whatever the stack frame happened to contain; MSCDEX ignores them for an IOCTL Output request.

Parameters:
  lock -- door state to request: 1 locks the drive door, 0 unlocks it. Taken as a single byte from the first stack argument and written straight into the second byte of the MSCDEX Lock/Unlock Door control block.

Returns:
  Nothing. Whether the drive accepted the command is left in the request status word at DAT_00069e20.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ailv3.lib symbol set, and the body reaches fdps_cd_device_request, the game's own MSCDEX plumbing, which no vendor library object could call into]

Rebuild note:
The terminating JMP looks like a tail call to a helper, but 0x0003c56b is a label inside FUN_0003c51c, so a rewrite cannot call it -- both C functions must carry their own copy of that tail, including the part that latches the request header's status word into DAT_00069e20. Drop that latch from either one and fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy afterwards reports on whatever request ran before, silently.

=== 0003c803 [PLATE]
Resolves the disc address range of the CD-ROM track that fdps_cdrom_read_track_info queried last, publishing it in the play-range globals so the caller can hand that range to the Play Audio request.

Algorithm:
Copies the queried track's start address out of DAT_00069e01 into the range-start global DAT_00069dec. Reads the queried track number from DAT_00069dff and the disc's highest track number from DAT_00069e07, the latter published by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info. When track + 1 is past the highest track the queried track is the last one on the disc, so the range end DAT_00069de4 takes the lead-out address DAT_00069e0b and the routine returns. Otherwise it calls fdps_cdrom_read_track_info for track + 1, which republishes DAT_00069e01 as the next track's start address; that value becomes the range end in DAT_00069de4, and a second call to fdps_cdrom_read_track_info for the original track number puts the track-info globals (DAT_00069e01, DAT_00069dff, DAT_00069e05) back on the track the caller had selected. The range end is exclusive: fdps_cd_play_audio_range takes the pair as (start, end) and sends end - start as the sector count of the Play Audio request. Every fdps_cdrom_read_track_info call is a real MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request, so the non-last-track path costs two extra device requests.

The closing restore call is state hygiene, not a dependency: no reader anywhere in the program observes what it republishes. DAT_00069e01 is read only here and in fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, DAT_00069dff only here and at fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors:0003c1b4, DAT_00069e05 only in fdps_cd_track_is_audio -- and each of those reads follows that function's own track query. fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors runs the same idiom, saving the selected track at 0003c1b4 and restoring it at 0003c1ff, so the shared CD state block is treated throughout as caller-owned state a helper must put back.

Parameters:
  none -- the track acted on is whichever one fdps_cdrom_read_track_info queried last, held in DAT_00069dff.

Returns:
  Nothing. The result is the pair DAT_00069dec (range start) and DAT_00069de4 (range end, exclusive); both callers read those globals immediately after the call.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom libraries or ailv3.lib; shares the CD track-state globals with fdps_cd_play_track and fdps_cd_stop_audio, and carries the PUSH n / CALL __CHK prologue of compiled game code]

Rebuild note:
The second fdps_cdrom_read_track_info call at 0003c851 must be kept even though nothing reads the globals it restores. It is a real MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request to the drive, so dropping it as dead code -- the obvious simplification once you notice DAT_00069e01/DAT_00069dff/DAT_00069e05 have no surviving reader -- changes how many device requests a track change costs. The same restore appears in fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors at 0003c205 and is equally unobserved; both are the CD block's convention of putting the shared track selection back, and both stay.

=== 0003c85b [PLATE]
Starts CD-DA playback of a single track: halts any audio in progress, selects the requested track, resolves its start and end positions, then issues the play request for that range.
Pool: fdps  [no library match; game CD-audio module]
Evidence: Function ID is empty against both the Watcom libraries and ailv3.lib (0 candidates either side, hash unique in the image), so no vendor bytes. All four callers are game CD routines (fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll, fdps_cd_verify_disc_and_play_track, FUN_00030bf0) and it calls fdps_cd_stop_audio plus the FUN_0003c0c8 / FUN_0003c803 / FUN_0003c452 cluster that shares the globals at 00069de4 and 00069dec. Neither CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387 nor Miles AIL 3.02 does red-book track control, and 55 bytes of parameterised logic is no linker island. The only vendor symbol touched is __CHK, the Watcom stack probe.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code, describing the observed sequence; no library symbol identified.
Boundary: 0003c85b-0003c891, entry is the PUSH 0xc / CALL __CHK probe, the RET follows the ADD ESP,0x8 that balances the frame, and 0003c892 opens the next function with the same probe prologue; gap_after is empty.
Signature: __cdecl void fdps_cd_play_track(short track) - the argument is read with MOVSX from [ESP+4] and the plain RET leaves cleanup to the caller; EAX is never set deliberately, so the return is void.
Body: 1. PUSH 0xc; CALL __CHK, the stack-overflow probe for 12 bytes (it pops its own argument, so ESP is unchanged on return). 2. CALL fdps_cd_stop_audio to halt any track currently playing. 3. MOVSX of the 16-bit track argument, passed to FUN_0003c0c8 which selects/queries the requested track (caller cleans the 4 bytes). 4. CALL FUN_0003c803, the only writer of 00069dec and 00069de4; it derives the playback start and end positions for the selected track (00069de4 is written on two paths, so the end position is conditional). 5. PUSH [00069de4] then [00069dec] and CALL FUN_0003c452, which therefore receives (start, end) and performs the actual play request; the 8 bytes are cleaned here.

=== 0003c892 [PLATE]
Starts CD-DA playback of a run of consecutive CD tracks, from the start of the first track through to the end of the last, and reports how long that run is.

Algorithm:
Halts whatever is playing with fdps_cd_stop_audio. Selects first_track with fdps_cdrom_read_track_info and calls fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, which publishes the selected track's start sector in DAT_00069dec and its end sector in DAT_00069de4; the start sector is latched out of DAT_00069dec here, because the second resolve overwrites both globals. Repeats the same pair for last_track and keeps only the end sector from DAT_00069de4. Hands the two latched sector numbers to fdps_cd_play_audio_range(start_sector, end_sector) as one continuous play request, then returns end minus start.

Parameters:
  first_track -- 1-based CD track number playback starts at, the same numbering fdps_cd_play_track and fdps_cdrom_read_track_info take; read sign-extended from a 16-bit stack slot.
  last_track -- 1-based CD track number playback stops at. Its end sector bounds the range, so this track is played in full. Not checked against first_track.

Returns:
  The length of the play range in CD sectors (frames), end sector minus start sector. It comes out negative when last_track precedes first_track, since neither argument is validated.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom 10.0x or the ailv3.lib set; game-side CD audio sequencing over the CD state globals shared with fdps_cd_play_track]

Rebuild note:
fdps_cd_resolve_track_range rewrites both DAT_00069dec and DAT_00069de4 on every call, so the start sector has to be read after the first resolve and before the second. Issuing both resolve calls and then reading the two globals -- the obvious way to write it -- yields last_track's start sector and plays the wrong range.

=== 0003c8e6 [PLATE]
Plays the whole game CD as audio: everything from the first sector of the disc through to the lead-out.

Algorithm:
Probes 12 bytes of stack with __CHK, then silences any playback in progress with fdps_cd_stop_audio. Asks the drive for track 1's audio track info through FUN_0003c0c8(1), which refreshes the track-info globals -- track number at 0x00069dff, track start sector at 0x00069e01, control byte at 0x00069e05 -- none of which this routine reads back. Calls fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info to refresh the disc summary; that leaves the highest track number in DAT_00069e07 and the lead-out address, converted to a logical sector number, in DAT_00069e0b. Finally hands (0, DAT_00069e0b) to fdps_cd_play_audio_range, which issues MSCDEX Play Audio (command code 0x84) starting at sector 0 for DAT_00069e0b sectors: the whole disc from its very first sector, not from where track 1's audio begins. That last call is reached by a JMP to 0x0003c889 -- the identical three-instruction tail of fdps_cd_play_track, which the compiler merged with this one. No code in the program calls this routine.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no library match in either the watcom or the ail Function ID set; its callees, the CD state globals it shares and its merged tail are all game CD code]

Rebuild note:
The obvious C rewrite passes track 1's start sector as the beginning of the play range, because the call that resolves it sits two lines above; the original passes the literal 0, so playback starts at the very first sector of the disc (the data track on this game's mixed-mode CD) rather than where track 1's audio begins. Write the 0 literally and keep the FUN_0003c0c8(1) call whose result is discarded.

=== 0003c911 [PLATE]
Reports whether one CD-ROM track holds CD-DA audio rather than data.

Algorithm:
Probes 8 bytes of stack through the Watcom __CHK stub, then calls fdps_cdrom_read_track_info with the track number. That routine issues the MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request with control block 0x0b (Read Audio Track Info) for the track and leaves the track's Q-channel ADR/control byte, masked with 0xd0, in DAT_00069e05. This function reads DAT_00069e05 back and returns whether it differs from 0x40, the masked control value of a data track; every audio-track control value survives the mask as something else. The other fields fdps_cdrom_read_track_info publishes for the track -- its Red Book start address at DAT_00069e01 and its track number at DAT_00069dff -- are left for other callers and are not looked at here.

Nothing in the shipped image calls this: it is part of the unused API surface of the CD-ROM module, half of whose functions are linked in but never referenced.

Parameters:
  track -- CD-ROM track number, as the MSCDEX audio-track-info control block takes it; a signed 16-bit value, the same argument fdps_cd_play_track forwards to fdps_cdrom_read_track_info.

Returns:
1 when the track is an audio track, 0 when it is a data track.

Pool: fdps  [no FID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; the PUSH 0x8 / CALL __CHK prologue is what the compiler emits for game source, and the body reads the game's CD globals]

Rebuild note:
The function has no result of its own to hand back: it depends on fdps_cdrom_read_track_info having just written DAT_00069e05, so a rewrite must keep both the call and the global. Folding the two into one function that returns the control byte would break fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors and fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, which call the same routine and pick different fields (DAT_00069e01, DAT_00069dff) out of the same globals. The test is also an exact equality against the masked byte -- CMP 0x40 after the callee's AND 0xd0 -- not a bit test; write the equality the binary writes rather than the `(control & 0x40) == 0` that reads more naturally, which is equivalent only for the Red Book-legal control values and only while the callee's mask stays 0xd0.

=== 0003c93a [PLATE]
Reads how far CD-DA playback has got: asks the CD-ROM driver for the audio Q-channel and hands the caller the track now playing and the running time inside that track.

Algorithm:
Calls fdps_cd_read_q_channel on the 11-byte MSCDEX IOCTL-input control block at 0x00069e56; that routine stamps control code 0x0c (Audio Q-Channel Info) into the block, wraps it in a 26-byte DOS device request (length 0x1a, subunit 0, command 3) and issues it through fdps_cd_device_request, so the driver's reply comes back in the same block. Four byte fields of the reply are then copied out through the caller's pointers, in the order the code writes them: block+2 (TNO, the track playing now) to *track, block+6 (FRAME) to *frame, block+5 (SEC) to *second, and block+4 (MIN) to *minute. The MIN store is not spelled out here: AL is loaded with block+4 and the body jumps to 0x0003bc71, the shared "MOV EDX,[ESP+8] / MOV [EDX],AL / RET" tail that sits inside fdps_cd_unpack_msf, which stores through the same second-argument slot and returns. The MIN/SEC/FRAME triple is the position within the current track; the driver reports the absolute position on the disc at block+8..+10 and this routine does not read it. Nothing in the program calls this entry.

Parameters:
  track -- pointer to the byte that receives the number of the track playing now (Q-channel TNO field).
  minute -- pointer to the byte that receives the minutes of the running time within that track.
  second -- pointer to the byte that receives the seconds of that running time, 0-59.
  frame -- pointer to the byte that receives the frames of that running time, 0-74 (1/75 second each).

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in any library; it drives MSCDEX through fdps_cd_device_request, and no CRT or AIL routine does that, while its PUSH 0x8 / CALL __CHK prologue marks compiled project C]

Rebuild note:
This routine reads the Q-channel FRAME field at block+6 even though the request its callee issues declares a 6-byte transfer, so block+6 is one byte past what the driver was asked to fill. Both halves of that mismatch have to survive a rebuild untouched: do not 'fix' the count on the fdps_cd_read_q_channel side (the owner of that literal 6), and do not drop or guard the frame read here on the grounds that the byte looks untransferred. Writing either the obvious count or the obvious validity check changes what the game asks the CD driver for and what it reports back.

=== 0003ca49 [PLATE]
Allocates a block of DOS conventional memory through DPMI INT 31h function 0100h and page-locks it, handing the caller the block's linear address, its real-mode far pointer and its protected-mode selector.

Algorithm:
Builds a Watcom union REGS on the stack with eax = 0x100 (DPMI Allocate DOS Memory Block) and ebx = paragraphs, and issues it with int386(0x31, &in, &out). When out.cflag is non-zero the allocation failed: the routine leaves every out-parameter untouched and returns 0. Otherwise it publishes the returned real-mode segment (out.eax) three ways -- *out_real_mode_ptr = seg << 16, the far pointer seg:0000; *out_linear = (seg & 0xffff) << 4, the flat linear address of the same byte; *out_selector = out.edx & 0xffff, the protected-mode selector DPMI created alongside the block and the handle fdps_dpmi_free_dos_memory needs to give it back. It then locks the whole block into physical memory with fdps_dpmi_lock_region(linear, linear + paragraphs * 16 - 1), recomputing the start as *out_real_mode_ptr >> 12 and the byte size as paragraphs << 4, and discards that call's result. Returns 1.

Parameters:
  paragraphs -- size of the block in 16-byte paragraphs, passed to DPMI in BX and multiplied by 16 to get the byte size of the locked range. Comes from the Miles AIL driver loaders, sized from a driver image.
  out_linear -- receives the flat linear address of the block (segment * 16). Written only on success.
  out_real_mode_ptr -- receives the block as a real-mode far pointer, segment in the high half and offset 0 in the low half. Written only on success.
  out_selector -- receives the protected-mode selector DPMI allocated for the block, the argument fdps_dpmi_free_dos_memory takes. Written only on success.

Returns:
  1 when the DPMI allocation succeeded, whether or not the page lock did; 0 when DPMI returned with CF set, in which case none of the three out-parameters has been written.

Pool: fdps  [game-written DPMI wrapper module -- the fn 0x100/0x101/0x600/0x601 group that the AIL vendor objects reach through EXTDEF; no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the AIL set]

Rebuild note:
The result of fdps_dpmi_lock_region is thrown away: this routine returns 1 whenever DPMI fn 0100h succeeded, even if the page lock failed, and on the failure path it leaves all three out-parameters untouched rather than zeroing them. Writing the obvious C -- return fdps_dpmi_lock_region(...), or clearing the out-parameters up front -- changes what the AIL driver loaders see.

=== 0003cad2 [PLATE]
Frees a DOS conventional-memory block that DPMI function 0100h allocated, by handing DPMI back the block's selector.

Algorithm:
Reserves 0x38 bytes for an adjacent pair of Watcom union REGS -- the input register set at ESP+0x00 and the output set at ESP+0x1c, 0x1c bytes each (eax, ebx, ecx, edx, esi, edi, cflag). Stores 0x101, the DPMI Free DOS Memory Block function code, into the EAX slot, and selector & 0xffff into the EDX slot at ESP+0x0c, which is where fn 0101h expects the selector. Calls int386(0x31, &in, &out) to issue the DPMI services interrupt and drops its three arguments with ADD ESP,0xc. No other slot of the input set is written, so the remaining registers enter the interrupt holding whatever the stack already contained; fn 0101h reads only AX and DX. The output set is never examined -- the carry flag at ESP+0x34 is discarded, so a failed free is silent. The prologue is a bare SUB ESP with no stack probe.

Only the third argument is read. The first two are the linear address and the real-mode far pointer of the same block, carried for symmetry with the three-output allocator at 0x0003ca49; AIL_internal_install_driver_inner, AIL_internal_uninstall_driver_inner, AIL_internal_dig_driver_teardown and AIL_internal_dig_driver_setup_full all push the three values out of the driver descriptor fields at +0x08, +0x00 and +0x04 that the allocator filled.

Parameters:
  linear_unused -- protected-mode linear address of the block, as the allocator at 0x0003ca49 wrote it (real-mode segment << 4). Never read.
  segment_unused -- the block's real-mode far pointer, segment in the high 16 bits and offset zero, as the allocator at 0x0003ca49 wrote it (real-mode segment << 16). Never read.
  selector -- the DPMI selector that fn 0100h returned for this block. Masked to 16 bits and loaded into DX; the only argument the body uses.

Returns:
  Nothing. The DPMI carry flag is discarded, so callers cannot distinguish a failed free from a successful one.

Pool: fdps  [the game's own DPMI service module, which the AIL vendor objects reach across the EXTDEF seam; no Function ID hit in either library, and it reaches the interrupt through the public int386 API rather than an inline INT, which is how a client uses the runtime and not how the runtime is built]

Rebuild note:
The vendor AIL objects call this with three pushed dwords and ADD ESP,0xc, so the rebuild must define all three parameters even though only the third is read. Writing the obvious one-argument free(selector) still links and, being __cdecl, still balances the stack -- but the body then reads the block's linear address where the selector should be, and because the DPMI carry flag is discarded every DOS low-memory free fails silently instead of reporting an error.

=== 0003cb01 [PLATE]
Locks a range of linear memory into physical memory through DPMI function 0x0600, so the pages stay resident while interrupt-time code touches them.

Algorithm:
Reserves a 0x38-byte stack frame holding a Watcom union REGS in/out pair (in block at ESP+0, out block at ESP+0x1c). Normalizes the two endpoints with an unsigned compare (CMP start,end and the two JNC arms), so callers may pass them in either order: base = min(start, end) lands in EAX and size = max(start, end) - base + 1 in EDX. The +1 means end is read as the address of the last byte of the range, not one past it. Stores 0x600 -- DPMI Lock Linear Region -- into the in block's EAX slot, then base>>16 and base&0xffff into the EBX and ECX slots and size>>16 and size&0xffff into the ESI and EDI slots, which is how fn 0x0600 takes its starting linear address in BX:CX and its byte count in SI:DI. The EDX slot is never written. Calls int386(0x31, &in, &out), then tests the out block's carry-flag word at ESP+0x34 and returns 1 when it is zero.

The stretch from 0x0003cb24 to the RET is a shared tail: fdps_dpmi_unlock_region at 0x0003cb6e does the same endpoint arithmetic, stores 0x601 instead, and jumps into 0x0003cb24 rather than carrying an epilogue of its own.

Parameters:
  start -- one endpoint of the linear byte range to lock, a flat address inside the LE image or in BSS. Callers pass the first byte of a code extent (0x4478c, 0x4b370, 0x477f4), the address of an AIL module static, or, from fdps_dpmi_lock_size, that function's base argument.
  end -- the other endpoint, also a flat linear address. The larger of the two is treated as the last byte of the range. fdps_dpmi_lock_size passes base + size here, so a block requested as (base, size) is locked as size + 1 bytes.

Returns:
  int -- 1 when the DPMI host returned with the carry flag clear, i.e. the range is locked; 0 when the call failed. fdps_dpmi_lock_size passes it straight back to its own caller; the AIL module-init routines and FUN_0003ca49 discard it.

Pool: fdps  [the game's own DPMI service module, which the vendored AIL objects reach across the EXTDEF seam -- no FID hit in either the Watcom or the AIL library set, and FD2 carries the same six-wrapper module in the same order at the same sizes]

Rebuild note:
end is the last byte of the range, not one past it: the byte count sent to DPMI is (max - min) + 1, so writing the obvious size = end - start locks one byte less than the original. It bites through fdps_dpmi_lock_size, which passes end = base + size and therefore makes the original lock size + 1 bytes -- when base + size falls exactly on a page boundary the original pins one page more than the caller asked for, and a rebuild that drops the +1 leaves that page pageable under an interrupt handler. Also keep the return sense inverted from the hardware: 1 means carry clear, i.e. success.

=== 0003cb6e [PLATE]
Unlocks a DPMI-locked range of linear memory so its pages may be paged out again; the counterpart of the fn 0x0600 lock primitive fdps_dpmi_lock_region.

Algorithm:
Normalizes the two endpoints with an unsigned min/max (CMP start,end then the two JNC arms reading the same flags), so callers may pass them in either order: base = min(start, end) in EAX, size = max(start, end) - base + 1 in EDX. The +1 means end is treated as the address of the LAST byte of the range, not one past it. Stores 0x0601, DPMI Unlock Linear Region, into the EAX slot of a 0x38-byte union REGS in/out pair built on the stack, then jumps to 0x0003cb24, the shared tail inside fdps_dpmi_lock_region: that tail writes base>>16 and base&0xffff into the EBX and ECX slots and size>>16 and size&0xffff into the ESI and EDI slots (DPMI fn 0x0601 takes the starting linear address in BX:CX and the size in SI:DI), calls int386(0x31, &in, &out), and returns 1 when the out block's carry-flag word came back zero.

This body has no epilogue of its own. The ADD ESP,0x38 and the RET that end the call both belong to fdps_dpmi_lock_region; the only instruction that distinguishes the two entries is the 0x0601 store here versus the 0x0600 store there.

The in block is never cleared before use: only the EAX, EBX, ECX, ESI and EDI slots are written, so the EDX slot reaches the DPMI host holding stack garbage. Fn 0x0601 ignores EDX, so this is harmless. Like the rest of this module the body carries no __CHK stack probe and no EBP frame, and it destroys EBX without saving it.

Parameters:
  start -- one endpoint of the linear byte range to unlock, a flat address in the LE image or in BSS. Callers pass the start of a code extent (0x477f4, 0x45203) or, through fdps_dpmi_unlock_size, the base of a static data block.
  end -- the other endpoint, also a flat linear byte address. The larger of the two is taken as the last byte of the range. fdps_dpmi_unlock_size passes base + size here, so a range requested as (base, size) is unlocked as size + 1 bytes.

Returns:
  int -- 1 when the DPMI host cleared the carry flag, i.e. the range was unlocked; 0 on failure. The six AIL_internal_dpmi_unlock_* callers discard it; fdps_dpmi_unlock_size passes it back to its own caller unchanged.

Pool: fdps  [the game's own DPMI service module, which AIL reaches across the EXTDEF seam -- no FID hit in either the Watcom libraries or ailv3.lib, and FD2 carries the same six-wrapper module in the same order and the same sizes]

Rebuild note:
Three ways the obvious C diverges here. (1) end is the address of the last byte of the range, not one past it: the size sent to DPMI is (max - min) + 1, so writing the obvious size = end - start unlocks one byte less than the original. It matters because fdps_dpmi_unlock_size passes end = base + size, which makes the original unlock size + 1 bytes -- when base + size lands exactly on a page boundary the original releases one page more than the caller asked for, and a rebuild that drops the +1 leaves that page locked. (2) The return sense is inverted from the hardware: 1 means the carry flag came back CLEAR, i.e. success. (3) The module must be compiled with stack checking off (#pragma off (check_stack), as FD2 does for the same six functions): no member has a __CHK probe, and they run on the AIL driver-setup path where the probe must not fire. What need NOT be reproduced is the missing EBX save -- the original destroys EBX in a __cdecl body, but only AIL vendor code and the module's own wrappers call in, and they treat EBX as scratch anyway, so letting the compiler preserve it is strictly safer.

=== 0003cb93 [PLATE]
Locks a memory block described as base address plus byte size into physical memory, so DPMI will not page it out while interrupt-time code touches it.

Algorithm:
Adds size to base to form the far endpoint of the block, then calls fdps_dpmi_lock_region with (base, base + size). That primitive takes two inclusive endpoints and asks DPMI function 0x0600 (Lock Linear Region) for (max - min) + 1 bytes, so the extent actually locked here is size + 1 bytes, one more than the caller named. Its return value is left in EAX untouched and becomes this function's result.

Every caller is an AIL vendor object reaching across the EXTDEF seam: the four once-only module bring-up routines page-lock their own code extent and their interrupt-touched statics through it, and AIL_internal_alloc_and_commit locks each block it allocates. The (start, end) form of the same operation is fdps_dpmi_lock_region; the undo is fdps_dpmi_unlock_size at 0x0003cbaa, a byte-identical twin over fdps_dpmi_unlock_region.

Parameters:
  base -- linear address of the first byte to lock. Callers pass the address of an AIL static block, of a heap block just allocated, or the first byte of a code range.
  size -- length of the block in bytes. Callers pass plain object sizes (4, 0x18, 0x40, 0x48, 0x80, 0x100) or, for code ranges, end minus start.

Returns:
  The lock primitive's success flag, passed through unchanged: 1 when the DPMI call returned with the carry flag clear, 0 when it failed.

Pool: fdps  [the game's own DPMI service module; every caller is an AIL vendor object referencing it across the EXTDEF seam, which does not make it library code -- the bytes are absent from ailv3.lib and its primitive at 0x0003cb01 is game code]

Rebuild note:
fdps_dpmi_lock_size(base, size) locks size + 1 bytes, not size: it hands fdps_dpmi_lock_region the endpoint pair (base, base + size), and that routine locks (max - min) + 1 bytes. Writing the obvious base + size - 1 in the rebuild, or reimplementing the wrapper over a half-open range, locks one byte fewer than the original and can leave the last byte of an interrupt-touched buffer pageable. Second, the routine has no stack-probe prologue, matching every other member of the module; it is reached only from AIL driver-setup paths that must be safe outside a normal stack context, so a rebuild has to suppress the __CHK probe explicitly (#pragma off (check_stack)) rather than let the compiler insert one.

=== 0003cbaa [PLATE]
Unlocks a DPMI-locked block of linear memory described as (base, size), for callers that hold an address and a byte count rather than a pair of endpoints.

Algorithm:
Adds size to base to form the end address, pushes (base, base + size) and calls fdps_dpmi_unlock_region, then drops the two arguments with ADD ESP,8 and returns. EAX is not touched after the call, so fdps_dpmi_unlock_region's status is the return value. That callee orders the endpoint pair, computes end - start + 1 as the byte length, loads DPMI function 0x0601 (Unlock Linear Region) into a union REGS frame and falls into the shared int386 tail at 0x0003cb24, which is owned by the fn 0x0600 lock primitive at 0x0003cb01 and turns the returned carry flag into 0 or 1. Because the end address is inclusive, the region actually unlocked is size + 1 bytes long. No frame is set up and no stack probe runs.

Parameters:
  base -- linear address of the first byte of the block to unlock; callers pass either a malloc'd block pointer or the address of a module static.
  size -- size of the block in bytes; the values seen at the call sites are small object sizes such as 4, 0x40 and 0x80.

Returns:
  int, passed through from fdps_dpmi_unlock_region: 1 when the DPMI call returned with carry clear (the pages are unlocked), 0 when it failed. All four callers ignore it.

Pool: fdps  [the game's own DPMI service module, defined by the game and reached by the vendored AIL objects across the EXTDEF seam; no FID hit in either the Watcom or the AIL library set]

Rebuild note:
The end address handed to fdps_dpmi_unlock_region is inclusive -- it computes end - start + 1 -- so this wrapper unlocks size + 1 bytes, not size. Writing the obvious 'return fdps_dpmi_unlock_region(base, base + size - 1);' would change the region by one byte; keep the arithmetic as base + size. The routine also has no stack-probe prologue, matching its siblings at 0x0003cb01 and 0x0003cb6e; it is reached from AIL driver-setup paths, so a rebuild must suppress the __CHK probe (#pragma off (check_stack)) rather than let the compiler add one.

=== 0003cbc1 [PLATE]

=== 00043310 [PLATE]
Watcom C/C++ 10.0a 32-bit DOS startup body: identifies the host DOS extender, shrinks the DOS memory block, copies the PSP command tail and the program name, records the NO87 flag, zeroes BSS, then runs the registered initializers and enters __CMain.
Pool: crt  [cstrt386.obj, _TEXT offset 0x78, from CLIB3S.LIB]
Evidence: module cstrt386 in CLIB3S.LIB publishes _cstart_@0x000, __exit@0x28f, __do_exit_with_msg__@0x292 and __GETDS@0x2cc in _TEXT; anchoring _cstart_ at 00043298 puts those at 00043527, 0004352a and 00043564, all real function starts here, and the module's code resumes at offset 0x78, which is this address. Corroborated by the runtime state it owns - the whole Watcom low-globals block at 0006041c-00060458 (initial ESP, PSP and environment selectors, DOS version, host type, NO87 flag, command line and program name pointers) - and by its callees __InitRtns (0004dfa6) and __CMain (0004df4c). Raw INT 21h/INT 31h probing and segment-register juggling with no C prologue rule out fdps; no AIL data or driver structures rule out ail; 535 bytes of real work rule out binary_artifact.
Name: no public symbol of its own. cstrt386 publishes nothing at offset 0x78, and being hand-written assembly it emits no LPUBDEF static name to recover, so the file-static form L$N_<module>_<purpose> applies, ordinal 1 as the module's only unnamed body ahead of the first public. No Function ID hit exists (0 candidates in both the Watcom and the ail sets).
Boundary: 00043310-00043526, ending at the CALL __CMain at 00043522, which never returns; the bytes at 00043527 are the module's public __exit. The entry proper is the 2-byte JMP at 00043298 that wears _cstart_, with the copyright data at 00043299-0004330f between it and this body.
Signature: no C convention. Hand-written assembly entered by JMP, never called; takes no stack arguments, cleans nothing up and never returns. The only incoming state read is loader-supplied: EDX (Intel Code Builder info block) and GS (DPMI selector). Any recorded void(void) prototype is a placeholder, assumed.

Algorithm:
  1. STI, align ESP down to a dword boundary, record the initial stack pointer
     at 00060434 and 00060420, preload selector 0x24 into 0006042c and EBX with
     'PHAR' for the Phar Lap probe.
  2. INT 21h AH=30h (get DOS version); AL/AH are stored as DOS major/minor at
     00060457/00060458. The high half of EAX selects the host:
       - 0x4458 ('DX'): Phar Lap 386|DOS-Extender. Version digit from BL; read
         the PSP memory-block end at ES:[5Ch] through selector 0006042c, round
         up to 4K, store at 00060420 and shrink the block with INT 21h AH=4Ah.
         Environment selector 0x2C.
       - 0x4243 ('CB'): Intel Code Builder. EDX points at the info block, saved
         at 000603ac; shrink memory by [EDX+1Ch] (INT 21h AH=4Ah), PSP pointer
         from [EDX+10h] (command tail at PSP+81h), environment segment from
         [PSP+2Ch] shifted left by 4.
       - otherwise: INT 21h AX=FF00h, DX=78h. If a host answers, this is the
         DPMI/DOS-4G path: a non-zero GS is saved at 000603b0, INT 31h AX=0006h
         fetches the DS segment base, the PSP selector comes from ES and the
         environment selector from ES:[2Ch]. If nothing answers, fall back to
         the fixed selectors (PSP 0x24, environment 0x2C, flat data 0x17).
     The host type/subtype pair goes to 0006044e/0006044f, the environment
     pointer to 00060451 and its selector to 00060455.
  3. Self-modifying step: with the flat data selector in ES, store DS into the
     code at 0004356d, the operand of the MOV DS,CS:[4356Dh] in the exit path.
  4. Command line: read the tail length from PSP:80h, skip leading spaces with
     REPE SCASB, copy the rest with REP MOVSB to the 16-byte aligned buffer
     past the end of BSS (0006a3bc rounded up), append two NUL bytes. That
     aligned buffer address is recomputed at the end and stored at 00060424,
     so 00060424 is the pointer to the copied command line.
  5. Environment scan: a string whose first four bytes lowercase to "no87" and
     whose fifth byte is '=' increments the no-x87 flag at 0006044c. After the
     terminating double NUL, skip the word count and copy the program name over
     the last NUL of the command line buffer; the address of that copy goes to
     00060428 and the first free byte past it to 00060430, the stack pointer to
     0006041c.
  6. Zero BSS from 00063930 to 0006a3bc with REP STOSD plus a byte tail; when
     the host type byte at 0006044e is 1 the cleared span is clamped to 0x1000
     bytes.
  7. CALL __InitRtns (0004dfa6) with EAX=0FFh to run every registered
     initializer up to priority 255, clear EBP, then CALL __CMain (0004df4c),
     which builds argc/argv, calls main and exits. __CMain does not return, so
     this call is the last instruction of the routine.
Open question: FD2 records the same vendor routine as one 557-byte function including the entry JMP and the copyright data; here it is split into _cstart_ at 00043298 and this body. That is an entity-layout difference only - both describe the same stock cstrt386 code, which is vendor-linked and not rebuilt from C.

=== 00044789 [PLATE]

It pops the return address into EDX, drops it and all five slots with ADD ESP,0x18, reloads SS from DS, sets ESP to the new top, recreates the caller's frame depth (SUB EBP,ESP captures the depth, MOV EBP,ESP / SUB ESP,EAX re-applies it), re-opens the five argument slots with SUB ESP,0x14 so the caller's own cleanup balances, and leaves by JMP EDX rather than RET. Only the depth is recreated, not the contents, so the caller resumes with a fresh EBP on a different stack and cannot reach its old locals -- the caller must be hand-written assembly too. The restore half at 00044e0f re-opens its three slots the same way (SUB ESP,0xc), so the idiom is the module's convention for the pair. Ghidra's recorded __watcall void(void) is an ANALYSIS guess the assembly refutes.
Neither half of the use32 pair is referenced anywhere in this image: both were dragged in with the whole ail_code.obj module, so no call site exists to confirm the contract against, and none is expected. This costs nothing for the rebuild because the AIL side is linked as a library rather than emitted as C.

PUSHAD lays down EAX..EDI; the two PUSHes add the ES and DS dwords on top; word [EBP-6] is the high half of the DS dword, exactly where __int7 stores SS (MOV word ptr [ESP+2],SS); and [EBP+0x0c] is the ESP slot of the PUSHAD block, exactly where __int7 stores the interrupted ESP. So the incoming frame holds, at entry ESP, +0x18 the interrupted ESP, +0x1c the interrupted SS (word), +0x20 ES and +0x24 DS, above the EIP/CS/EFLAGS that POPAD leaves ESP pointing at for the IRETD. These are values the extender's frame supplies because a ring-3 client's ESP and segments cannot be read out of the handler's own registers -- which is why this variant exists at all, and why the offsets reach past a plain same-privilege frame. The two pushed dwords do double duty: arguments to the core on the way in, and the values popped back into DS and ES on the way out.
Boundary: 0004eba8-0004ebc8, ends at the IRETD; the 3 bytes after it (87 db 90) are alignment padding before __int7_X32VM.
Signature: No C calling convention. Entered on vector 7, it reads nothing from EAX/EDX/EBX (all saved by PUSHAD, restored by POPAD), takes its inputs from the trap frame, and leaves via IRETD. The recorded __watcall(EAX, EDX, EBX) was Ghidra's guess and is not what the assembly does.

=== 00056799 [PLATE]

=== 000567a0 [PLATE]
Blocks until the player presses a key, then discards every scancode still queued by the keyboard ISR.

Algorithm:
Spins re-reading the scancode ring's read index at 0x00070019 and comparing it against the write index at 0x0007001d, looping while the two are equal, which is the queue-empty condition. fdps_keyboard_isr advances the write index every time it queues a make code, so the loop falls through on the first key press. The routine then stores the read index into the write index, rewinding the queue to empty: the key that ended the wait and anything else pending are thrown away, so the screen that follows does not inherit them. That is the same single store the flush-without-waiting routine at 000567b3 makes. The ring itself is the 10-entry byte buffer at 0x0007000f, dequeued by the routine at 000567be.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  void. EAX is left holding the read index as a by-product of the compare; no caller reads it.

Pool: fdps  [shares the scancode ring with the game's own INT 09h handler; no Function ID hit in any library]

=== 000567b3 [PLATE]
Discards every keyboard scancode still queued by the game's INT 09h handler, without waiting for one.

Algorithm:
Loads the read index of the keyboard ring from 0x00070019 and stores it into the write index at 0x0007001d, leaving the two equal. fdps_keyboard_isr advances 0x0007001d as it appends scancodes to the 10-entry byte ring at 0x0007000f, and the queue-pop function at 000567be advances 0x00070019 as it takes them out, reporting an empty queue (0xff) whenever the two indices match; rewinding the write index onto the read index therefore makes every scancode already in the ring unreachable. Nothing else is touched -- the ring bytes, the last-scancode byte at 0x00070006 and the ISR's repeat-suppression byte at 0x00070021 keep their values. The sibling at 000567a0 is the blocking form of the same operation: it spins until the indices differ and only then performs this identical store.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  nothing; EAX is left holding the read index as a side effect of the load and no caller reads it.

Pool: fdps  [shares the keyboard ring globals with the game's own INT 09h handler, which the Watcom CRT and AIL never own; no Function ID hit in either library set]

=== 000567be [PLATE]
Takes the next scancode out of the keyboard queue that fdps_keyboard_isr fills, or reports the queue empty.

Algorithm:
Sets the no-key marker 0xff in AL first, then loads the queue's read index from 0x00070019 and compares it with the write index at 0x0007001d; equal indices are the queue-empty condition and the routine returns the marker untouched. Otherwise it reads the byte at 0x0007000f + read index -- the 10-entry ring that fdps_keyboard_isr appends make codes to -- then increments the read index and stores 0 back when the increment reaches 10, the ring length. Only the read index is written, so it never contends with fdps_keyboard_isr, which owns the write index and the ring bytes. 0xff cannot collide with a real entry because fdps_keyboard_isr queues nothing with bit 7 set, i.e. no break codes. The same ring is emptied without reading by fdps_flush_keyboard_queue, and by fdps_wait_any_key after it has blocked for one key.

Parameters:
  none

Returns:
  The dequeued scancode, 0x01..0x7f, or 0xff when nothing is queued. Only AL is set; the upper 24 bits of EAX keep whatever the caller left in them, and every call site masks the result with AND EAX,0xff before using it.

Pool: fdps  [shares the scancode ring globals with the game's own INT 09h handler; no Function ID hit in either library set, and all callers are game-side interactive loops]

Rebuild note:
The ring has no fullness test: fdps_keyboard_isr advances the write index unconditionally, so after ten unread scancodes the write index catches up to the read index and this routine reports the queue empty while ten bytes sit in it. Writing the obvious ring buffer -- a pending count, or a full check that drops the incoming byte instead -- changes which keystrokes the game sees; keep the two bare indices with 'equal means empty' and the 0xff marker.

=== 00056898 [PLATE]
Computes the FDE.SAV integrity checksum: the unsigned sum of every byte of the save image except its trailing 4-byte checksum field.

Algorithm:
Hand-written assembly. Loads save_image into ESI (and, unused, into EDI), sets ECX = size - 4 so that the trailing 4-byte checksum field is left out of the sum, zeroes EBX (the accumulator) and EAX, then loops LODSB / ADD EBX,EAX for ECX iterations, adding each byte zero-extended to 32 bits. Moves EBX into EAX and returns. EBX is used as the accumulator without ever being saved or restored, and the MOV EDI,ESI is dead: both are consequences of sharing its shape with fdps_xor_crypt_buffer, which sits immediately after it at 000568b7 and does use EDI, for STOSB. ECX is a LOOP count, so a size of exactly 4 would iterate 2^32 times; every call site passes 0x59cb.

Parameters:

  size -- total size of the image in bytes, counting the trailing 4-byte checksum field; 0x59cb at every call site.

Returns:
  The 32-bit sum of the first size-4 bytes. fdps_load_savegame and fdps_title_screen compare it with the dword stored at save_image+0x59c7 and treat a mismatch as a corrupt save; FUN_000241e0 and fdps_battle_system_submenu write it to that dword before scrambling the image with fdps_xor_crypt_buffer and writing the file out.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in any library, hash unique in the image, four game callers and no callees; the hardcoded 'length minus 4' skip is a game data-format detail no CRT routine has, and 31 bytes of loop logic is neither a thunk nor a linker island]

=== 00056a0d [PLATE]
Blit mode 0: decodes an RLE 4-op pixel stream into an 8bpp destination surface, writing every pixel it draws through unchanged.

Algorithm:
Per row it loads the row width from DAT_00070024 into BX, then reads one command byte from ESI at a time until that counter reaches exactly zero. The top two bits of the command byte select the op, the low six bits carry len-1, so len = (cmd & 0x3f) + 1, i.e. 1..64:
  00 fill      -- reads one pixel byte from the stream and REP STOSB writes it over len destination bytes; width -= len.
  01 stretched -- reads one pixel byte and writes it into every second destination byte across a 2*len span (INC EDI then STOSB, so the second byte of each pair is written and the first is left holding whatever was already there); width -= 2*len.
  10 literal   -- REP MOVSB copies len bytes straight out of the stream; width -= len.
  11 skip      -- EDI += len with no write, i.e. a transparent run; width -= len.
When the row width hits zero it adds the end-of-row advance in EDX to EDI, decrements the row counter at DAT_00070022, and restarts at the entry, which reloads a fresh row width. It returns once that row counter reaches zero.

Op 01 is not a half-tone: replaying all 99 .CEL sheets shipped with the game (28,467 sprites) finds only 791 of these runs, 746 of them one pixel long, and their start column is even 462 times and odd 329 times, so nothing aligns them to a pixel pair. What they actually produce is a single untouched column immediately left of the pixel they write -- and 642 of the 838 untouched columns have a written pixel on their other side too, i.e. a one-pixel hole punched into otherwise solid content (M050.CEL sprite 17 row 2 is a fully painted tile row with one such hole at column 11). Two bytes buy what a skip-then-literal pair would cost three, so this is the encoder's packing of 'leave one column, then one pixel', and the hole it leaves is part of the original's output.

This is the kernel fdps_blit_dispatch calls for mode 0, the plain sprite and tile blit. fdps_rle_blit_mirrored_vertical (mode 8) reuses this same body bottom-up: it points EDI at the last raster line and tail-jumps here with a negated row stride in EDX. fdps_rle_blit_remap_sprite_and_backdrop (mode 1) and fdps_rle_blit_with_palette_remap (mode 2) decode the identical four ops but push every pixel through a 256-entry remap table.

Parameters:
  none on the stack. This is hand-written assembly; every input arrives in a register or a global, all of them set up by fdps_blit_dispatch immediately before the call:
    ESI          -- RLE command stream, advanced in place past the bytes it consumes
    EDI          -- destination pixel pointer, advanced in place
    EDX          -- end-of-row advance, computed by the caller as pitch - width
    ECX          -- must be zero on entry; the body writes only CL but reads all of CX/ECX
    DAT_00070024 -- u16 row width in pixels, reloaded at the top of every row
    DAT_00070022 -- u16 rows remaining, decremented to zero by this routine

Returns:
  nothing. EAX, EBX, ECX, ESI and EDI are all destroyed.

Pool: fdps  [no fid hit in either library, and it shares the blit width/height globals with fdps_blit_dispatch, which calls it as blit mode 0]

Rebuild note:
This kernel cannot be written as an ordinary C function: it takes ESI (stream), EDI (destination) and EDX (row advance) in registers, destroys EBX, ESI and EDI, which Watcom's convention says a callee preserves, and it requires the upper 24 bits of ECX to be zero on entry -- fdps_blit_dispatch does XOR ECX,ECX at 0005690d for exactly that. The body only ever writes CL, but then uses the whole of CX in SUB BX,CX and the whole of ECX in REP MOVSB / REP STOSB / LOOP, so a caller that skips the zeroing gets runaway runs that overrun the destination. A second trap is the row terminator: OR BX,BX / JNZ ends a row only on an exact zero, so hardening it to 'width <= 0' changes behaviour on any stream whose last run overshoots the row. A third is op 01: the obvious reading of a 'stretched fill' is that it doubles each pixel across the 2*len span, and writing it that way paints the columns the original leaves alone. The original writes only the second byte of each pair (INC EDI before STOSB) and the gaps really do stay as they were -- measured on the shipped sheets, most of those gaps are one-pixel holes inside painted content, so filling them changes what the game draws.

=== 00056a39 [EOL]
3-byte NOP padding (90 90 90)

=== 00056a53 [EOL]
3-byte 0x90 NOP alignment gap inside FUN_00056a0d's address range

=== 00056a6f [EOL]
3-byte 0x90 NOP alignment filler

=== 00056a8d [PLATE]
RLE sprite blit kernel, mode 1 of fdps_blit_dispatch: draws one RLE 4-op pixel stream through a 256-entry palette remap table and puts the destination pixels showing through the sprite's transparent runs through the same table, so every pixel of the width x height rectangle ends up as remap[...].

Algorithm:
Entered by a plain CALL from fdps_blit_dispatch (0005692d, the CMP BH,0x1 arm) with that function's registers still live: ESI = the RLE command stream, EDI = the destination pixel, EDX = pitch - width (the end-of-row advance), EAX and ECX zeroed, and EBP still the dispatcher's frame pointer. The first instruction overwrites EBP with [EBP+0x1c], the dispatcher's sixth argument, which here is the base of the 256-byte palette remap table. Each row starts by loading BX with the row width from DAT_00070024, then decodes command bytes until BX is exactly zero. A command byte's low six bits give len = (byte & 0x3f) + 1 (1..64) and its top two bits select the op:
  0b00 RLE fill -- read one stream byte, write remap[byte] to len destination pixels with REP STOSB; BX -= len.
  0b01 stretched fill -- read one stream byte, write remap[byte] to len pixels spaced two apart, the first landing at EDI+1; BX -= 2*len.
  0b10 literal copy -- for each of len stream bytes write remap[byte]; BX -= len.
  0b11 backdrop recolour -- consume no stream byte; for len pixels read the pixel already at EDI, write remap[that pixel] back and advance; BX -= len. This is the op that the kernels at 0x00056a0d (mode 0) and 0x00056b25 (mode 2) implement as a transparent skip (ADD EDI,ECX).
Every lookup is MOV AL,byte ptr [EAX + EBP*0x1] with EAX holding nothing but the pixel byte, so the table index stays in 0..255 only because the dispatcher zeroed EAX; ECX likewise carries the run length for REP/LOOP only because the dispatcher zeroed it. When BX reaches zero the row ends: EDI += EDX, the remaining-row counter DAT_00070022 is decremented, and the outer loop reloads BX for the next row. The routine returns when DAT_00070022 reaches zero.

Place in the kernel family:
The thirteen kernels split into pairs on this one op. fdps_rle_blit_with_palette_remap (mode 2) applies the same remap table but leaves the transparent runs alone; fdps_rle_blit_tint_sprite_and_backdrop (mode 0xa) and fdps_rle_blit_tint (mode 0xb) are that same pair with a tint blend in place of the table lookup. This kernel is the remap half of the "affect the backdrop too" side.

Nothing in the shipped executable selects mode 1. Every path that can reach the dispatcher's mode argument resolves to a constant: 31 direct call sites pass 0, eight pass 9, two pass 8, one passes 0xb; fdps_draw_scene_layer passes 9 or 0xa; fdps_blit_unit_sprite passes its caller's 3 or 0; fdps_cel_blit_sprite passes its own eighth argument, a literal 0 at 50 call sites and 4 at the other four; and fdps_draw_tilemap_cell passes the draw request's +0x20 field, which the eighteen callers of fdps_draw_composite_sprite set to 0, 3 or 9 and which fdps_draw_composite_sprite itself replaces with 0 or 9 per part when it arrives as 0. No entry in that chain has a non-call reference, so no function pointer can bypass the census. The modes that reach the dispatcher are 0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 0xa and 0xb; 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 0xc are compiled in and unreachable.

Parameters:
  none on the stack -- the inputs arrive in registers and globals prepared by fdps_blit_dispatch:
  ESI -- base of the RLE command byte stream, pointing past the caller's header.
  EDI -- destination address of the first pixel of the first row, in an 8bpp linear surface.
  EDX -- pitch - width, added to EDI at the end of every row.
  EBP -- on entry the dispatcher's frame pointer; [EBP+0x1c] is its sixth argument, the 256-byte palette remap table, and EBP is replaced by that pointer for the rest of the body.
  DAT_00070024 -- row width in pixels, reloaded once per row.
  DAT_00070022 -- number of rows still to draw, decremented once per row.

Returns:
  nothing. EAX, EBX, ECX, ESI, EDI and EBP are all left modified; in particular the caller's frame pointer is destroyed, which fdps_blit_dispatch survives only because it unwinds through ESP-relative POPs.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; the only caller is fdps_blit_dispatch, and 0x00070022/0x00070024 are that dispatcher's blit parameter block, not library state]

Rebuild note:
The row terminates only on the width counter hitting exactly zero (SUB BX,CX then OR BX,BX / JNZ), so a stream whose runs overshoot the row width does not stop -- BX wraps and the decoder keeps painting past the end of the row; writing the obvious while (remaining > 0) in C would end the row early and silently change what a malformed or deliberately over-long stream draws. The stretched-fill op writes its first pixel at dst+1, not dst (INC EDI before STOSB at 00056ad1), so the run occupies the odd columns of its 2*len span; the obvious for (i = 0; i < len; i++) { dst[0] = c; dst += 2; } shifts the whole run one pixel left. And the 0b11 op is not the transparent skip it is in most of the family: copying the mode-0 or mode-2 body and only swapping the table in leaves the backdrop inside the sprite's bounding box unremapped.

=== 00056abf [EOL]
3-byte 0x90 NOP alignment filler

=== 00056adc [EOL]
3-byte 0x90 NOP alignment filler

=== 00056afd [EOL]
3-byte 0x90 NOP filler inside the FUN_00056a8d address range

=== 00056b25 [PLATE]
Blit mode 2 of fdps_blit_dispatch: draws one RLE-coded sprite into the destination surface, passing every pixel it writes through a 256-byte palette translation table. No call site in the shipped program ever asks for mode 2, so this kernel is unreachable in FDPS.LE; see Reachability.

Algorithm:
Takes the translation table base out of the caller's frame slot [EBP+0x1c] (fdps_blit_dispatch's arg6) into EBP, destroying its own EBP for the rest of the call. Then, per destination row, it loads the row width from the 16-bit global at 0x00070024 into BX and decodes control bytes from ESI until BX reaches exactly zero. A control byte's low six bits are a length minus one, so len = (b & 0x3f) + 1 (1..64), and its top two bits select the run:
  00 -- fill: read one source byte, write table[byte] to len consecutive destination pixels (REP STOSB); charges len columns.
  01 -- stretched fill: read one source byte, write table[byte] to len pixels at stride 2 starting at dst+1 (INC EDI / STOSB / LOOP), leaving the pixels in between untouched; charges 2*len columns.
  10 -- literal: read len source bytes and write table[byte] for each; charges len columns.
  11 -- skip: advance the destination by len pixels without writing, i.e. transparency; charges len columns.
At the end of a row EDI advances by EDX, the end-of-row slack (pitch - width) that fdps_blit_dispatch computed, and the 16-bit row counter at 0x00070022 is decremented in place; the routine returns when that counter reaches zero, leaving the global at 0. The stream format is the game's four-opcode RLE, the same one the untranslated mode-0 kernel fdps_blit_rle_passthrough decodes; the mode-1 kernel fdps_rle_blit_remap_sprite_and_backdrop uses the same table but spends its 11 opcode recolouring the pixels already in the destination instead of skipping them, and the mode-3 kernel fdps_blit_rle_recolor replaces the table lookup with an arithmetic recolour of every pixel.

Reachability:
Mode 2 is never selected. Every one of the 26 static callers of fdps_blit_dispatch was enumerated; the literal mode bytes pushed are 0, 8, 9 and 0x0b, and the four call sites that pass a variable resolve as follows:
  fdps_cel_blit_sprite -- forwards its eighth stack argument (the argument at [EBP+0x2c] becomes the dispatcher's arg6, not the mode). Across all 54 of its call sites that eighth argument is the literal 0 (50 sites) or the literal 4 (4 sites).
  fdps_blit_unit_sprite -- forwards its blit_mode argument, which is the literal 3 at two call sites and 3 or 0 in fdps_flash_units_in_color.
  fdps_draw_scene_layer -- never forwards its layer_mode at all: it only compares it with 0 and 1, and pushes 0x0a when it is 1 and 9 otherwise. The layer_mode byte itself comes from byte +0x1c of the 0x20-byte per-layer record in dscNN.dat (Field2.vfs), which across the shipped data holds 1 for 62 layers, 0 for 3 and 2 for one (DSC07.DAT layer 1) -- but that 2 is a layer flag, not a blit mode, and never reaches the dispatcher.
  fdps_draw_tilemap_cell -- forwards field +0x20 of the 0x24-byte SAF draw request, and every one of the seventeen builders of that record writes that field with the literal 0, 3 or 9.
Nothing takes the address of fdps_blit_dispatch, so there is no indirect path into it. The modes the game actually asks for are 0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 0x0a and 0x0b; modes 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 0x0c are compiled in and unreached. Consequence for the rebuild: this kernel cannot be exercised by playing the game, so a transcription error in it will not surface in playtesting.

Parameters:
  none in the C sense -- the routine takes no stack arguments. Its inputs are registers set up by fdps_blit_dispatch: ESI = the RLE stream, EDI = the destination pixel address, EDX = pitch - width, and EBP = the caller's frame pointer, whose +0x1c slot holds the translation table base. EAX and ECX must arrive with their upper 24 bits clear (the dispatcher's XOR EAX,EAX / XOR ECX,ECX at 0005690d), because the table index is the whole of EAX and REP STOSB, LOOP and ADD EDI,ECX use the whole of ECX. Row width and row count come from the 16-bit globals at 0x00070024 and 0x00070022 that the dispatcher wrote. The table is 256 entries: the index is a zero-extended source byte.

Returns:
  nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the ailv3 set; the sole caller is the game's blit dispatcher, and this body reads back the same 0x00070022/0x00070024 blit-geometry words that dispatcher writes, so writer and reader are one module]

Rebuild note:
The stretched-fill run (opcode 01) writes its first pixel at dst+1, not at dst -- the loop is INC EDI then STOSB -- so the obvious rewrite `for (i = 0; i < len; i++) dst[i*2] = c;` shifts every stretched span one pixel to the left. The row is also terminated by a 16-bit counter tested for exactly zero (SUB BX,CX / OR BX,BX / JNZ), and opcode 01 subtracts len twice, so a run that overshoots the remaining row width wraps through 65535 and keeps decoding; rewriting the test as `while (width > 0)` on an int quietly changes that behaviour. Neither mistake can be caught by playing the game: no call site in the program selects mode 2, so this kernel has to be got right by reading rather than by testing.

=== 00056b57 [EOL]
3-byte 90 90 90 alignment filler after an unconditional jmp inside FUN_00056b25

=== 00056b74 [EOL]
3-byte NOP filler between a JMP at 00056b72 and the branch target at 00056b77

=== 00056b95 [EOL]
